# Lifecycle flows audit 006: Claude Fable report

[Audit 006](README.md) · [Audit directory format](../README.md)

- **Auditor:** Claude Fable 5.2, orchestrating Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude
  Sonnet 5.5 agents, each given an explicit model and effort.
- **Date:** 2026-11-18.
- **Audited commit:** `91f6e71b9`, read from a frozen worktree.
- **Scope:** everything `bootwright apply` and `bootwright destroy` do, from
  the command line to the last durable write: the lifecycle engine, the
  operation and context stores, the adapter runner and protocol, every
  capability in Go, and the embedded Ansible collection's roles, playbooks,
  action plugins, modules and utilities that those capabilities run; the
  commands an operator uses around a failure (`status`, `logs`, `plan`,
  `diff`, `context delete`); the operator guide and the end-to-end runbooks;
  and the private operation logs of 29 retained real runs.
- **Questions:** the owner asked for the weak and unsafe points of the two
  flows; the loose ends from which an operator cannot recover; a way for
  Bootwright to have a meta view of those points and handle them; how the
  output informs the operator when the commands fail; and a plan. While the
  audit ran the owner added that these operations should be a state machine,
  so that the possible scenarios are predictable.
- **Result:** 380 verified findings (16 High, 126 Medium, 238 Low) from 62
  review lanes, with 14 candidates refuted; a map of 1,247 families of
  failure points and 497 implicit states; a design for the meta view; and a
  plan of seven workstreams.

This report changes no product code, specification, milestone or decision.
It authorizes no implementation and no command with effects. Every
recommendation in it, the plan included, is a proposal for the owner.

## 1. Verdict

**The two flows are safe and hard to break, and hard to understand when
they stop.** The engine underneath `apply` and `destroy` proves before it
acts, orders every durable write for the crash, and recovers from a kill at
any point without the operator knowing it happened. What it does not do is
explain itself: when a step fails, the cause the automation worked out
rarely reaches the operator, is kept nowhere, and the next command printed
is often the one that fails again. The owner's two instincts are both
right. The stops are not mapped: 1,170 places in the Go code raise a
lifecycle failure and three codes cover 96% of them. And the flows are
already a state machine at their core, tested as one, with everything
around that core left to prose and control flow.

### 1.1 What is strong and must be kept

- **It fails closed.** Every refusal of a decision comes before any effect,
  and everything decided is proved again under the exclusive lock.
- **It survives the crash.** No cut between two durable writes of an apply
  or a destroy led to a dead end; each leaves a condition the next command
  recognises. The tests already kill at every write.
- **It never guesses an outcome.** An effect whose result is not known
  blocks everything until it is observed; an interrupt never erases what an
  attempt proved.
- **The unsafe surface is small.** Sixty-two lanes found 13 unsafe points,
  two of them High, and no path by which a destructive step acts without
  its proof, outside the name-derived ownership of the libvirt arm.
- **The core is already declared and tested.** One pure decision rule, five
  transition tables in the spec, and a test that drives the code with every
  row.

### 1.2 What needs work

In order of importance:

1. **The cause of a failure does not reach the operator, and is not kept.**
   A role that fails without naming one of 55 declared reasons ends as "the
   adapter operation did not complete", whatever its task said; every role
   failure in the retained real runs read that way ([C17-01](#c17-01)). Nothing durable
   records why an attempt failed, so `status` cannot say it an hour later
   ([O08-01](#o08-01)). In 41% of the mapped failure points the cause is
   visible nowhere, and in 15% only in the private operation log
   ([section 7](#7-what-the-operator-is-told)).
2. **A stop has no identity.** Three codes cover 1,124 sites; 72% of the
   messages are fixed sentences that cannot name the object they are about;
   65% of the `lifecycle.state` sites give no remedy and fall back to "run
   status" ([section 2](#2-measured-baseline)). Nothing can be documented,
   counted, scripted on or tested per stop.
3. **The flows are a state machine only at their core.** Of 497 conditions
   the code distinguishes, 364 appear in no table; about fifteen decisions
   are taken around the tested rule; the recovery from interruptions is
   correct and spread over many files
   ([section 3](#3-the-flows-as-they-are)).
4. **Dead ends are reached without warning.** Fifty were verified. Most are
   where a deliberate policy ends, and the operator is not told so: a target
   that is gone, a build that was updated, a record that cannot be read.
   The exit that exists is not named, and the remedy printed loops
   ([section 6](#6-dead-ends-and-loose-ends)).
5. **A short list of unsafe points**, led by a Secret binding that an
   interrupted additive apply releases by mistake ([E05-01](#e05-01)) and
   by removals that trust a name ([X09-02](#x09-02), [X09-03](#x09-03))
   ([section 5](#5-weak-and-unsafe-points)).
6. **Tests pin the safe behavior, not the operator's text.** The failure
   goldens render hand-written diagnostics, no golden covers a failed
   destroy, and the kill harness does not drive additive, paused or relaxed
   operations ([X13-06](#x13-06), [X13-03](#x13-03)).

### 1.3 The ten actions that matter most

1. Fix the Secret-binding release, with a test that fails first
   ([E05-01](#e05-01)).
2. Keep the cause: write the first diagnostic of every failed, unknown or
   canceled attempt into its record and its log, and let `status` show it
   ([O08-01](#o08-01)).
3. Put each cause on its block: name the block, the object and the step
   that was running, keep the engine's order, and let the last failure read
   as a consequence ([O01-05](#o01-05), [O02-01](#o02-01)).
4. Give every adapter ending its own text: an exit status, a signal, a
   deadline, a hangup, a death before the request was loaded
   ([E06-01](#e06-01), [E10-02](#e10-02)).
5. Add the safety net for role failures: the failing task's name, its step,
   its host and its kind, for every role, without converting any
   ([C17-01](#c17-01)).
6. Make every remedy a command that works from the state it is printed in,
   and name the last exit where one stop may never clear
   ([X16-02](#x16-02), [X04-01](#x04-01), [X04-02](#x04-02),
   [E09-03](#e09-03)).
7. Declare the stops: one catalog, one code per stop, the state it leaves,
   its recovery and its exits, with a test that no lifecycle failure is
   raised outside it, and an `explain` command
   ([section 8](#8-the-meta-view-the-flows-as-one-explicit-state-machine)).
8. Name the states and let the tables decide: the conditions a cut leaves,
   the guards around the decision rule, one writer of the operation state;
   then check that no stop leads in a circle and every cut leaves a named
   state ([X14-03](#x14-03), [X14-02](#x14-02)).
9. Close the name-derived ownership gaps the backlog already holds, and
   the smaller exposures ([X09-02](#x09-02), [X09-03](#x09-03),
   [X10-03](#x10-03), [C06-03](#c06-03)).
10. Decide the exits for a target that is gone and for a build update, and
    fix the traps inside single capabilities
    ([section 10](#10-decisions-for-the-owner), [C01-01](#c01-01),
    [C07-01](#c07-01), [C10-01](#c10-01)).

Actions 2 to 5 answer the complaint that started this audit and need no
decision. [Section 9](#9-plan) turns all ten into seven workstreams with an
order, sizes and exit evidence.

## 2. Measured baseline

Every figure in this section was measured for this audit at `91f6e71b9`, with
small tools written for it and kept out of the repository
([section 11](#11-method-verification-and-limits) describes them). None of
these figures is a gate today.

### 2.1 How many ways the flows can stop, and how they are told apart

A diagnostic is built in Go by a call whose first argument is its code, or by
a composite literal with a `Code` member. Counting those sites in the
production Go under `internal/` and `cmd/`:

| Measure | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Diagnostic emission sites, all codes | 1,511 |
| Sites in the lifecycle area (`lifecycle.*`, `runtime.internal`, `runtime.log`) | 1,170 |
| of which `lifecycle.state` | 886 |
| of which `lifecycle.unknown` | 129 |
| of which `lifecycle.unsupported` | 109 |
| of which `lifecycle.authorization` | 17 |
| of which `lifecycle.stage` | 10 |
| of which `runtime.internal` | 10 |
| of which every other lifecycle code together | 9 |

Three codes carry 1,124 of the 1,170 sites (96%). A code therefore tells an
operator, a script or a support request almost nothing: `lifecycle.state`
alone covers 886 different conditions, and only the sentence beside it tells
them apart.

The sentence is the real identity, and it is not treated as one:

| Message of a lifecycle site | Sites | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| One fixed sentence (a string literal) | 847 | 72% |
| Built at run time (it interpolates a name, a value or another message) | 320 | 27% |
| None | 3 | 0% |

The 847 fixed sentences are 771 distinct texts, so nearly every site already
has its own wording; it simply has no name, no number, no documentation entry
and no test that pins it to a meaning. A fixed sentence also cannot name the
object it is about: 116 distinct sentences open with "a" or "an" ("a managed
libvirt network is not active", "a machine disk is not the size the profile
froze") in code where the frozen request holds the name.

### 2.2 What the operator is told to do next

`internal/diagnostics/remediation.go` gives each code a default remedy, used
when a site supplies none.

| Remedy of a lifecycle site | Sites | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| None of its own (the code's default applies) | 607 | 52% |
| A fixed sentence | 281 | 24% |
| Built at run time (usually an exact command) | 277 | 24% |
| Not applicable | 5 | 0% |

For `lifecycle.state` alone, 579 of 886 sites (65%) carry no remedy, so the
operator reads the default:
`run bootwright status --context <context> to see the records and the next step`.
[Section 7](#7-what-the-operator-is-told)
shows that `status` cannot answer that question for a failed block, because
nothing durable records why the block failed.

The sites are not spread evenly. The engine itself writes specific messages
and exact commands; the capabilities do not:

| Area | Lifecycle sites | Fixed sentence | No remedy of its own |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `internal/storage/ceph` | 330 | 247 | 119 |
| `internal/reconciliation/lifecycle` | 174 | 81 | 46 |
| `internal/substrate/libvirt` | 126 | 121 | 101 |
| `internal/managedos/installation` | 120 | 84 | 70 |
| `internal/containercluster/agentinstall` | 71 | 60 | 55 |
| `internal/substrate/kubevirt` | 55 | 43 | 48 |
| `internal/reconciliation/ansiblerunner` | 52 | 45 | 32 |
| `internal/infrastructureservices/mirrorfill` | 36 | 16 | 20 |
| `internal/managedos/diskdiscovery` | 31 | 27 | 21 |
| `internal/managedos/physicalerase` | 29 | 24 | 8 |
| `internal/substrate/baremetal` | 25 | 18 | 18 |
| `internal/managedos/hostfirewall` | 20 | 12 | 20 |
| Every other package together | 101 | 69 | 49 |

### 2.3 The Ansible side

Most effects run in the embedded collection, so most real failures start
there. Counted in the roles' task files:

| Measure | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Named tasks | 1,440 |
| Tasks under `no_log: true` | 651 (45%) |
| `assert` tasks | 199 |
| `fail` tasks | 107 |
| Tasks with `failed_when: false` (judged by the next task) | 104 |
| `rescue` sections | 9 |
| Protocol emissions: `loaded` 78, `group` 125, `completed` 82, `prepared` 4 | 289 |
| Protocol emissions of a named `refused` reason | 55 |

The adapter result protocol lets a role end with a named `refused` reason, for
which Go holds a message and a remedy. Only 55 emissions do. Every other
failing task, the 306 `assert` and `fail` tasks included, ends the playbook
with a non-zero exit, and the runner turns every such exit into the same
diagnostic: `lifecycle.state`, "the adapter operation did not complete"
(`internal/reconciliation/ansiblerunner/process_linux_amd64.go:510`). The
role's own message stays in the retained raw output, which is a root-owned
file, and for 45% of the tasks `no_log` removes it from there too.

### 2.4 What is kept about a failure

The durable records are precise about what happened and silent about why.
The [operation records](../../specs/state-reconciliation.md#operation-records)
contract lets only a resolution whose observation could not run carry a
`failure` member, "an optional member no other record carries". An attempt
record therefore holds the outcome word and nothing else, and the attempt log
agrees: in the retained logs of real runs the line that closes a failed
attempt reads `"event":"outcome","detail":"failed"`. Once the terminal output
has scrolled away, no command can say why a block failed.

### 2.5 What real runs looked like

The owner's end-to-end runs keep their private operation logs. The audit read
29 archives of them (the same operation often appears in several archives, so
the figures below count each operation once).

| Measure | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| Operations (apply or destroy) | 65 |
| Invocations of those operations | 154 |
| Operations that completed in one invocation | 36 |
| Operations that needed two | 14 |
| Operations that needed four to six | 13 |
| Operations that needed eleven or more | 2 (11 and 16) |
| Operations with at least one attempt that did not succeed | 18 (28%) |
| Attempts recorded | 1,877 |
| Attempts that ended `changed` or `unchanged` | 1,791 |
| Attempts that ended `failed` | 16 |
| Attempts that ended `canceled` | 41 |
| Attempts that ended `unknown` | 29 |
| Resolutions that followed | 86: `partial` 49, `no-effect` 16, `unknown` 16, `completed` 5 |
| Blocks that needed two or more attempts | 43 |

Two things stand out. First, of the 86 attempts that did not succeed, 70 (81%)
ended unproved, `canceled` or `unknown`, and each of those costs a resolution
before anything else may run: in practice an operator who hits a problem
usually meets the unknown path, not the simpler failed path. Second, the
non-successes concentrate in a few kinds of block: operating-system
installation (45 of 218 attempts: 12 failed, 33 canceled), Ceph host
preparation (13 of 117 unknown) and Ceph cluster bootstrap (5 of 33 unknown).

What those logs kept as the reason, where they kept one at all, reads like
this (identifiers redacted):

```text
lifecycle.unknown: the Ceph host preparation could not prove its
remote-refusal boundary (adapter detail:
native-unknown:ValueError@ceph_native_worker.require:<line>)

the installation of Machine <m> on Machine <m> is not what its apply froze:
the installation adapter did not prove its postcondition

lifecycle.state: the adapter operation did not complete
```

[Appendix D](#appendix-d-real-run-incidents) lists the incidents the two
real-run lanes reconstructed, with the cause each one really had.

| --- | ---: |
| 1 | 240 |

| The exit the stop leaves | Families | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |

| Run the other verb | 129 | 10% |
| Fix the input, then repeat | 102 | 8% |
| Only the build that registered the operation can go on | 90 | 7% |

So 268 families, about one in five, leave the operator without an ordinary
exit, and for more than half of all families the output does not say what
happened clearly enough to act on (clarity 1 or 2).

### 2.7 How much of the flows is an explicit state machine today

The engine has a real, tested core. `classify` in
`internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/transitions.go` is one pure rule over the
requested verb and six facts about the operation the context holds, with
eight outcomes; `internal/reconciliation/state.go` holds the attempt,
resolution and operation-precedence rules as pure functions; and
`TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec` drives all of them from the five tables of
[the state machine section](../../specs/state-reconciliation.md#state-machine).

Around that core the flows are prose and control flow. The lanes named every
distinguishable condition the code branches on that no table lists:

| Implicit states the lanes reported | States |
| --- | ---: |
| Named by a spec transition table | 14 |
| Named in part | 119 |
| Named by no table | 364 |
| **Total** | **497** |

The two lanes that extracted the machine itself found that `classify` decides
about a third of what a verb does over the durable state it meets; about
fourteen further decisions are early returns around it, the operation record
has five separate writers, and three state variables of a removal (how far a
fresh removal has got before it registers, which of its releases a completed
removal still owes, and why a removal paused) have no durable name at all.
A draft of both machines as implemented lists 173 states and 319
transitions; the spec's tables cover 98 of the transitions (31%).
[Section 3](#3-the-flows-as-they-are) gives the detail.

## 3. The flows as they are

This section describes what `apply` and `destroy` do today, in the order they
do it, and what is left when they are cut. It is the ground the findings and
the proposed machine stand on. It follows the two lanes that walked every
durable write ([X01](#lane-x01), [X02](#lane-x02)), the two that extracted the
state machine ([X14](#lane-x14), [X15](#lane-x15)) and the engine lanes;
[Appendix E](#appendix-e-the-machine-as-implemented) holds the full tables.

### 3.1 Apply, write by write

A fresh apply makes about 23 durable writes across six stores (the operation
store, the mutation evidence, the controller state, Secret custody, the log
root and the job area under `/run`):

1. Under the shared lock it reads the index, the operation, its frozen plan
   and every block record, and decides (`decide`, then `classify`).
2. It presents the plan, confirms, and checks every `--authorize` token.
3. First exclusive transaction (`protect`): it re-proves what it decided
   from, claims an operation directory holding an empty `blocks/`, and raises
   the mutation evidence to running.
4. Outside any transaction it binds the Secrets the plan consumes and proves
   the bound material.
5. Second exclusive transaction (`register`): it re-proves the evidence and
   the exact list of claims, publishes the controller host binding, reserves
   host keys, then writes `plan.json`, `operation.json` and last `index.json`.
   The index write is the point of registration.
6. It opens the operation log.
7. For each block, as its dependencies complete: the block record
   (`pending`), the attempt record (`running`), the block record (`running`),
   the attempt log, a job directory under `/run` with the lent Secret files,
   then the adapter run and its remote effects, the preparation when the
   adapter publishes one, the retained output, the produced material into
   custody, the attempt record with its outcome, and the block record with
   its state.
8. It writes the operation's terminal state, projects it into the mutation
   evidence, and releases bindings no operation names.

Every record write is staged, synced, renamed, read back and its directory
synced; a failure after the rename is classed as possibly landed, never as
not written.

### 3.2 Destroy, write by write

A fresh destroy over an apply is a sequence of independently atomic
publications under the context lease; nothing spans them:

1. It decides under the shared lock, and finalizes first when a completed
   operation's records lag.
2. Under the lease it proves the controller host and re-proves what it
   decided from.
3. Over an apply that did not complete, it resolves every unproved block
   first: a resolution record, a read-only observation, a custody capture
   when the observation proves completion, the resolution's outcome, and the
   apply's own record again. This is the only writing a destroy does before
   it registers, and it writes into the apply it is about to supersede.
4. It refuses while a consumer would survive the removal or anything it takes
   back is still in use (the quiescence gate).
5. It raises the evidence, then writes the removal's plan, record and index.
6. For each block, in removal phases (online work, then stopped Machines,
   then the rest): the reservation is marked releasing, the attempt starts,
   any copy the inverse would delete is kept in custody first, the inverse
   runs, the attempt completes.
7. It records the removal done, withdraws produced material and releases
   reservations in that transaction.
8. Outside the lease it releases each Secret binding; a second lease then
   publishes pristine evidence and reclaims empty claims.

### 3.3 What a cut leaves, and who collects it

The lanes considered a kill, a power cut and a full disk between each
consecutive pair of those writes. For apply, no cut between two writes led to
a dead end: each leaves a condition the next `apply` or `destroy` recognises
and either collects or observes again. Destroy behaves the same, and its
tests already drive a kill at every write point.

| Condition a cut leaves | Left by | Collected by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A claimed directory holding only an empty `blocks/` | a kill after the claim | the next pristine publication, registration or settling destroy |
| Running evidence with no operation | a kill between the two registration transactions | the next apply's registration, or a destroy, which releases it first |
| A Secret binding no operation names | a kill after the bind and before the index | the next fresh registration, a removal's finalization or a settling destroy |
| A reservation with no operation | a kill after the reservations and before the index | the same |
| `plan.json` beside an empty `blocks/`, named by no index | a kill between the plan and the index | nothing: it is neither reclaimed nor reported ([X02-03](#x02-03)) |
| An index write that may or may not have landed | an I/O error on the index publication | the evidence and binding are kept; the next verb reads the index |
| A running attempt record the block record does not count yet | a kill inside the start of an attempt | the next start adopts it |
| A block `running` with no executor | a kill during the adapter run | the next verb observes it before anything else |
| An attempt record with a proved outcome beside a block record still `running` | a kill between the two outcome writes | the next verb observes the block again |
| An operation whose record is terminal and whose evidence is not | a kill between the two | finalization, before any verb |
| A removal recorded done whose releases did not finish | a kill or a failure after the record | finalization, by either verb |
| A latched log fault | a failed write under the log root | proved reopening of the log by the next invocation |
| Lent Secret files and scratch under `/run` | a kill of the elevated process | the sweep before the next adapter run on the host |

Two things in this table matter for the rest of the report. The engine
recovers from these conditions without the operator knowing they exist, which
is a strength: but none of them has a name an operator, a test or a message
can use. And the recovery is spread over many files as ad-hoc recognition
code, which is where the one defect of this kind sits: a failure between
registration and the end of an additive apply releases a Secret binding its
predecessor still needs ([E05-01](#e05-01)).

Effects on remote hosts are outside this table. A kill ends the local process
tree; an installer, a management controller or an orchestrator that already
received its order goes on. Only the capability's next observation stands
between that and a retry over work still in progress
([E10-06](#e10-06)).

### 3.4 The machine that is really there

The flows are a state machine with six levels. Only the middle of it is
written down as one.

| Level | Its states today | Where they are decided | In a spec table |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Context | pristine, claimed, registered, removal completing, protected with nothing an index accounts for, unreadable, lease held | prose in two spec sections; recognition code in `decision.go`, `registration.go`, `finalization.go`, the context guard | no |
| Lineage | an apply and the applies it adds to; the chain of removals that replace failed ones | `lineage.go`, `lineage_removal.go` | no |
| Operation | running, paused, failed, unknown, done | `classify` in `transitions.go` over the requested verb and six facts | yes |
| Removal phase | before registration: host proved, resolved, survivors checked, quiescent; after: online work, stopped Machines, the rest | `executor.go`, `removal_gates.go`, `removal_phases.go`; in memory only | no |
| Block | pending, running, failed, unknown, done | `state.go` | yes |
| Attempt or resolution | started, prepared, run, judged, outputs captured, recorded; five outcomes | `attempts.go`, `state.go` (only the last step: outcome to block state) | in part |
| Adapter run | loaded, prepared, groups, then one of 14 endings | `internal/adapterprotocol` (a closed enumeration) | in part, as prose |

What the tables hold is solid: `classify` is one pure rule with eight
outcomes, used by the decision, by finalization, by the next step `status`
names and by the reopening of a frozen binding, so those four always agree.

A draft of the two machines as they are implemented
([Appendix E](#appendix-e-the-machine-as-implemented)) puts numbers on the
rest. For apply it lists 89 states and 156 transitions, of which the spec's
tables cover 55; for destroy, 84 states and 163 transitions, of which they
cover 43. So the tables hold about a third of the transitions of apply and
a quarter of those of destroy, and nearly all of the uncovered ones are
failure, interruption and crash transitions.

What they do not hold:

- **About fifteen guards around `classify`.** The checks for records no index
  accounts for, a finalization that is due, an erase relaxation, lost block
  records, contradictions, the stage selection, the execution-contract and
  closure proofs, the host binding and the input drift are early returns
  before or after the rule, so their refusals and remedies are rows of no
  table; and one of the spec's own tables, the one that follows an apply
  observation with the removal's check, is not bound to the code by the
  conformance test ([X14-03](#x14-03)).
- **The steps inside a transition.** Registration is eight writes with a
  three-valued outcome (not registered, registered, possibly registered);
  an attempt is about ten steps; the completion of a removal is five
  (record, custody, reservations, bindings, pristine evidence) across two
  transactions and one loop over the keyring. Each "stopped after step k" is
  a real state, recognised somewhere, named nowhere.
- **The scheduler's stop conditions.** Six latches (an attempt that could
  not start, a block that failed again, the online boundary, the log fault,
  observe-only mode, the pre-stop phase) decide when an invocation stops
  admitting work. They are booleans in two functions.
- **How an ending becomes an outcome.** Which adapter ending is `failed`,
  which is `unknown` and which is `canceled` is decided in three files, in
  part by the diagnostic code of the error
  (`internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/invocation.go:299`).
- **The writers of the operation record.** Five places write the operation's
  state, each with its own derivation, and after a completion write fails
  the terminal write takes the block's state from the scheduler's memory,
  not from the record the precedence table names ([X14-02](#x14-02)).
- **Every stop itself.** No transition, tabled or not, carries the stop it
  raises: the message, the state it leaves and the exit are written at the
  site, 1,170 times ([section 2](#2-measured-baseline)).

So the answer to "could these operations be a state machine" is that they
already are one, by construction and by test at its core, and by convention
everywhere else. The proposal of [section 8](#8-the-meta-view-the-flows-as-one-explicit-state-machine)
is to finish what `classify` and its test started.

### 3.5 What is strong and must be kept

- **It fails closed, and it proves before it acts.** Every refusal of a
  decision comes before any registration or effect; everything decided under
  the shared lock is proved again under the exclusive one, down to each
  block's attempt count.
- **Every durable sequence is ordered for the crash.** The claim precedes
  the evidence, the plan precedes the index, the attempt record precedes the
  block record. A reader that meets any prefix knows what it is looking at.
- **Outcomes survive the interrupt.** Outcome records, releases and
  restorations run under a context that cancellation cannot reach, so Ctrl-C
  never erases what an attempt proved.
- **An unproved effect blocks everything until it is observed.** Nothing
  retries, depends on or removes an effect whose outcome is not known.
- **Finalization is monotone and idempotent.** Each step is its own atomic
  publication, a repeated step is harmless, and either verb finishes what
  the other left.
- **Produced material is never the first thing lost.** A custody failure
  after a proved effect records unknown, never failed, and an inverse that
  would delete the only copy of a kubeconfig keeps it first.
- **Process supervision is engineered end to end**: parent-death signals, a
  subreaper for session-isolated workers, job locks that tell a live sibling
  from leftovers, lent material removed only when no process holds the lock.
- **Locks cannot go stale.** Both are kernel locks on descriptors that close
  on exec, so a dead holder never blocks the next command.
- **The adapter protocol is closed.** Bounded canonical records, a closed
  list of refusal reasons, a detail grammar that cannot carry a value.

None of the changes this report proposes weakens any of these.

## 4. The failure-point map

[Appendix B](#appendix-b-failure-point-register) is the map: 1,247 families
of places where the flows can stop, one table per lane, each row giving the
trigger and its code site, the code and text the operator gets, the remedy,
whether the text names its target and shows its cause, the state left, the
exit, and a clarity score from 1 to 5. It is the raw material of the
catalog proposed in [section 8](#8-the-meta-view-the-flows-as-one-explicit-state-machine):
a family here becomes a stop there. Lanes overlap by design, so one stop can
appear in two lanes' tables; the map is a census taken from many sides, not
a deduplicated list.

Where the stops are, and how well each phase explains itself:

| Phase of the flow | Families | Mean clarity | Share scoring 1 or 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Confirmation and authorization | 28 | 3.9 | 14% |
| Context deletion | 16 | 3.2 | 18% |
| Decision | 197 | 3.1 | 35% |
| Registration | 79 | 3.0 | 30% |
| Invocation | 24 | 3.0 | 41% |
| Start of an attempt | 62 | 2.7 | 45% |
| Removal gates | 37 | 2.6 | 54% |
| Removal phases | 10 | 2.6 | 60% |
| Resolution | 81 | 2.5 | 51% |
| Finalization | 33 | 2.5 | 45% |
| Presentation | 75 | 2.5 | 54% |
| Produced material | 28 | 2.3 | 57% |
| Release | 20 | 2.2 | 55% |
| Adapter run | 418 | 2.2 | 68% |
| Recording an outcome | 35 | 2.1 | 77% |
| Evidence check | 80 | 2.0 | 82% |
| Other | 24 | 2.6 | 58% |

The pattern is plain. Where the engine refuses over a state it names
(authorization, decision, registration), the operator is told what happened
and what to run. The further a stop is from the engine's own vocabulary,
inside an adapter run, in the check of the evidence an adapter returned, in
the recording of an outcome, the less the operator learns: a third of all
families sit in the adapter run, and two thirds of those score 1 or 2.

Destroy is harder to leave than apply. Of the families that belong to
`apply` alone, 10% have no ordinary exit (they need the registering build,
a backup, manual work, abandoning the context, or have none); of those that
belong to `destroy` alone, 31%; of those common to both, 24%.

## 5. Weak and unsafe points

A finding is filed as unsafe when Bootwright can damage or lose data, act on
something it does not own, go on past an outcome it has not proved, expose
secret material, or record success for something not done. Sixty-two lanes
looked for these, and the list is short: 13 findings, 2 High, 6 Medium and 5
Low. Outside the name-derived ownership of the libvirt arm, described
first below, no path was found by which an `apply` or a `destroy` wipes the
wrong disk, removes another context's Machine, or reports a removal that did
not happen; the proofs before each destructive step hold.

The findings fall into five groups.

**Ownership proved by name.** The libvirt arm recognises what it owns by a
name it derives. A provider-host removal stops and removes its managed
networks without checking which guests use them, which breaks another
context's or a hand-made guest on a shared host ([X09-02](#x09-02)). A
Machine removal that finds no domain deletes the disk directory, the
controller unit and the container on the name alone ([X09-03](#x09-03)),
which matters when a context was recreated under the same name after an
orphan-acknowledged deletion; and the unattended form of that deletion
skips the warning about exactly this hazard ([X09-01](#x09-01)). Following
the "rename it" remedy for a domain misread as foreign leads to a destroy
that reports success while the renamed domain stays ([C02-04](#c02-04)).
The first three are recorded and parked; this audit adds that they are the
whole of the wrong-target surface it found.

**A Secret binding released by mistake.** An additive apply that fails
between its registration and the end of its run, through a store fault or
an interrupt in a short window, releases the Secret binding its predecessor
froze. The predecessor's lineage can then be neither continued nor removed
by Bootwright ([E05-01](#e05-01)). This is new, small to fix, and the first
slice of the plan.

**Effects that outlive the command.** A cancellation or a deadline ends the
local process tree. A worker already started on a managed host goes on, for
up to several minutes in the Ceph case, while the next observation may read
a half-done effect ([E10-06](#e10-06)).

**Access the controller depends on.** Starting firewalld locally on the
controller skips the proof of SSH admission that the same step makes for a
remote Machine, so new logins to the controller can be refused
([C06-03](#c06-03)).

**Secret material in view.** The token that guards the published recovery
passphrase and registration files is passed in the arguments of two
commands and can be read from the process table while they run
([X10-03](#x10-03)).

The remaining five are Low: unit names that two contexts can share, a
required-log fault that turns provable sibling outcomes into unknown, a
trust-slot rule, a power command that holds no claim on its controller, and
a retained physical Machine that always reads idle.

One more weakness belongs here although it is not a defect of any one line:

applies are not in its journeys ([X13-03](#x13-03)). Naming those states
and widening the harness is the structural answer
([section 8](#8-the-meta-view-the-flows-as-one-explicit-state-machine)).

## 6. Dead ends and loose ends

A dead end is a state an operator can reach from which no Bootwright command
recovers, or whose only exit is abandoning the context, an older build, a
restore from a backup, or work by hand on hosts or files. A remedy that
names a command which then refuses the same way counts too. The audit
verified 50: 4 High, 28 Medium and 18 Low.

Most of them are not accidents. Bootwright refuses rather than guesses, has
no force path and adopts nothing, and many of these states are where that
policy ends: the findings are labelled "policy trade-off" when the refusal
is deliberate. What the audit holds against them is narrower and holds in
nearly every case: the operator is not told that this is the end of the
road, the remedy printed loops or names something no command does, and the
one exit that exists is not named.

### 6.1 The families

**A target that is gone or silent.** If a hypervisor host died, a BMC was
replaced, or a hosted cluster's API will never answer again, the blocks on
it can be neither observed nor removed, and one such block refuses the
whole destroy. The decision to refuse is recorded and deliberate. The exit
is `context delete --purge --allow-orphans`, which abandons every object of
the context, not only the dead one, and the operator guide names it. The
refusals do not: an unreachable hypervisor is reported as a Machine "still
in use" with the remedy to stop it, which needs the same hypervisor
([X04-01](#x04-01)); a block left unknown on a lost host says "restore the
target, then repeat" ([X04-02](#x04-02)); a done block whose inverse must
reach the dead host fails every destroy, and the destroy that replaces it
tries the same inverse ([X04-03](#x04-03)); a hosted Machine behind a
broken host cluster is the same case one level up
([C04-02](#c04-02), [C04-04](#c04-04)).

**A build update.** This is the dead end an operator who does nothing wrong
is most likely to meet, because the usual reason to install a new build is
that the old one failed. A fix that moves an execution contract makes the
new build refuse to continue the operation, and to remove it; the remedy
names the build that registered it, and nothing keeps that build
([X06-01](#x06-01)). A refactor that only renames Go types moves the
contract fingerprint too ([X06-02](#x06-02)); a build made from a modified
tree records no mark of it, so the remedy can name a build nobody can
rebuild, or the running one ([X03-03](#x03-03)); the five wordings of the
other-build remedy name no command and never the deletion
([O06-08](#o06-08)).

**Traps inside one capability.** Each is a defect with a contained fix: a
provider host reached over SSH that lacks `virsh` crashes the first
observation before the task that would install it ([C01-01](#c01-01)); an
erase worker that refuses before its first status write looks alive for
more than four hours, then times out, and the remedy repeats the wait
([C07-01](#c07-01)); a Ceph consumer apply that ends unknown can never be
continued, because its observation can only answer "complete" or refuse
([C10-01](#c10-01)); a Ceph bootstrap cut before its first monitor exists,
and a package transaction cut part way, refuse on every repeat under a text
that does not name the exit ([C11-05](#c11-05), [C09-05](#c09-05),
[G02-02](#g02-02)); a consumer on physical Ceph hosts cannot be destroyed
and the plan gives no warning ([C10-04](#c10-04)); a discovery target left
running without its media is called foreign ([C06-02](#c06-02)); a
VirtualMachine edited on its host cannot be removed, because the check that
guards the removal demands the frozen shape ([C04-03](#c04-03)); a
placement host whose key changed strands its operation
([C16-03](#c16-03)).

**Records, the store and its bounds.** A refusal over an unreadable or
contradicted record sends the operator to `status`, which reads the same
record ([E09-03](#e09-03), [O03-02](#o03-02)). Damage to one context's
directory refuses every context, and the named exit is a whole-store
restore that nothing defines ([E11-03](#e11-03)). Finished operations are
never pruned, so a context that is destroyed and applied again often enough
ends at deletion ([X19-01](#x19-01)), and a removal keeps room for exactly
one pass, so a destroy forced by a full store cannot retry one failed block
([X19-02](#x19-02)).

**Rules that leave only destroy.** Once an update has changed a completed
apply's input, destroy is the only way on, even after the original bytes
are back ([E02-05](#e02-05)); an addition that cannot succeed can only be
dropped by destroying everything it was added to ([E04-03](#e04-03)).

**Remedies that loop.** A failed apply names `apply` as its next step also
when the role's own stop says this apply cannot proceed; in all three real
runs that hit it, the apply was repeated ([X16-02](#x16-02)). Bound-Secret
refusals at attempt time say to rebind and repeat, which reuses the bound
version ([G01-01](#g01-01)). "Inspect the cluster before repeating the
apply" cannot be done with Bootwright in that window ([C08-04](#c08-04)).

### 6.3 Loose ends

A loose end is something a failure leaves behind that nothing collects or
reports. Fifteen were verified, one Medium and fourteen Low. None corrupts
state; each is residue an operator may trip over later.

## 7. What the operator is told

This is where the flows are weakest, and it is the owner's own complaint: the
output of a failing `apply` or `destroy` does not say what happened. The
safety of the engine is not in question in this section; every stop described
here leaves the state consistent. What is missing is the explanation.

### 7.1 A failed apply, as it reads today

When a task of a role fails, the operator sees this (assembled from the
runner, the scheduler and the CLI golden
`internal/cli/testdata/cli-apply-failed.golden`; the two error blocks go to
standard error, the rest to standard output):

```text
  error  lifecycle.state
    the adapter operation did not complete
    Next: read blocks/machine-rhel-01/attempt-000001.output in this
          operation's Logs directory, as root, for why block machine-rhel-01
          failed
  error  lifecycle.state
    the apply did not complete
    Next: continue it with bootwright apply --context lab

  ! Apply failed

  Result
  Infrastructure
    [DONE] serve artifacts for lab-artifacts on controller
  Substrates
    [DONE] realize the libvirt host of lab-libvirt on controller
  Machines
    [FAIL] realize the virtual machine rhel-01 and its emulated BMC
    [PENDING] install the operating system of rhel-01

    Logs    /var/log/bootwright/contexts/lab/operations/op-<id>
    Follow  bootwright logs --context lab --operation op-<id>
    Next    bootwright apply --context lab
operation: op-<id>
verb: apply
state: failed
next: continue-apply
```

Measured against the five things an operator needs:

| Question | Answered? |
| --- | --- |
| What failed | In part: the `[FAIL]` row names the block. The error lines do not, and with two failed blocks nothing pairs an error with its row. |
| Where (which host, object, step, task) | No. The step that was running is erased when the row settles. |
| Why | No. The role often computed a precise cause, sometimes with the fix; it is in a root-owned file. |
| What state things are in now | In part: block states and the receipt. Not whether an effect may have happened. |
| What to do next | Often wrong: `Next` says repeat `apply`, also when the role's own message says only `destroy` can get past this. |

One hour later `bootwright status` shows the same `[FAIL]` row and no reason
at all, because the reason was never stored.

### 7.2 The defects behind it

The lanes reported 321 output findings; after duplicates were merged they
group into eleven defects. The first two account for most of what an operator
experiences.

**1. The role's own cause never becomes the diagnostic.** A role ends in one
of two ways: a named `refused` reason, which Go turns into a specific message
and remedy, or a failing task, which the runner turns into "the adapter
operation did not complete" whatever the task said
([C17-01](#c17-01)). Only 55 emissions are named. What is lost differs by
capability and is listed per capability: the installation's stops, some of
which say that only `destroy` helps ([C05-01](#c05-01)); the OpenShift
installer's diagnosis, host in error, stall, budget, DNS
([C08-01](#c08-01), [C08-02](#c08-02)); the disk discovery's own vocabulary
of causes ([C06-01](#c06-01)); the managed services' image
pull, unit start and listener causes ([C13-01](#c13-01)); the libvirt and
KubeVirt roles ([C02-01](#c02-01), [C04-01](#c04-01)); the physical claim's
identity mismatches ([C03-03](#c03-03)); add-on objects
([C15-01](#c15-01)); mirror fills ([C14-01](#c14-01)). The printed remedy
names a file to read "as root" where a supported reader exists,
`bootwright logs --raw --block` ([O10-03](#o10-03)).

**2. Nothing durable records why an attempt failed.** The attempt record may
not carry a failure and the attempt log keeps the outcome word only, so
`status` and `logs` cannot explain a `[FAIL]` after the run
([O08-01](#o08-01)). For failures Go itself raises (an evidence check, a Ceph
refusal) the text exists nowhere once the terminal is gone
([O07-02](#o07-02)). The operation log records only that an invocation opened
it, never what the invocation decided or where it stopped
([O09-06](#o09-06)).

**3. Censoring removes causes that carry no secret.** 45% of the tasks run
under `no_log`. A completion that proves no postcondition builds a message
from field names only, made to be safe, and its own task censors it
([C17-02](#c17-02)); a protocol publication that refuses its own arguments is
censored the same way ([O09-05](#o09-05)); Ceph roles publish their reason
only through the censored channel, and their remedy then sends the operator
to an output that holds the words "the run names its reason"
([O04-02](#o04-02), [O04-02](#o04-02)); six target-identity asserts show
their task name and neither the Machine nor the remedy, and rare erase
faults read as the generic failure ([X10-02](#x10-02), [X10-04](#x10-04)).

**4. One sentence, or one internal token, for many causes.** Ceph refusals
of very different kinds (not ready, a partial cluster, a transport failure,
a remote refusal) render through one template, "could not prove its
`<token>` boundary", with one remedy ([C10-03](#c10-03)); native tokens
outside a block's list of reasons publish as `remote-refusal` with a generic
remedy, and no catalog gives any token's meaning ([C11-04](#c11-04)); 63
Ceph evidence checks share one message ([C09-07](#c09-07)); when an unknown
attempt is read again, a postcondition flag is checked before the specific
checks, so the difference found reads "did not prove its postcondition"
([O07-01](#o07-01)); 54 package-source sites report the one token `packages`
([C12-09](#c12-09)); and most `lifecycle.state` sites leave the remedy to
the generic default ([O05-04](#o05-04)).

**5. Messages that name no object.** Evidence refusals say "a network", "a
disk" or "a daemon" with the frozen name in scope ([O07-05](#o07-05));
a block's failure diagnostics are forwarded without the block's identity,
although its warnings carry it, and are then sorted by code and message, so
concurrent failures cannot be matched to result rows ([O01-05](#o01-05));
Ceph cluster refusals never name the host that failed ([C09-01](#c09-01)),
OSD refusals neither the host nor the disk ([C09-09](#c09-09)); keyring
diagnostics no Secret, binding or file ([E12-03](#e12-03)).

**6. Environment faults are not classified.** The controller stage classifies
a failed download (dns, certificate, timeout, unreachable, proxy, status,
integrity, trust, storage). No other adapter does. An unreachable SSH target
or a changed host key ends as the generic failure ([X07-01](#x07-01)); a
Redfish 401 or 403 is reported as "did not answer" and recorded unknown
([C03-02](#c03-02)); a registry DNS failure on a Ceph host becomes a
"remote-refusal boundary" ([C12-03](#c12-03)); a full log root reads "restore
the directory" with the errno dropped, while a full state root names the
errno and the fix ([X01-02](#x01-02)); mirror fills fold route, credential,
DNS and disk-full into "unreachable" ([X07-07](#x07-07)); every `oc` failure
is "not answered", so a permanent 401 waits out the whole readiness budget
([C15-03](#c15-03)).

**7. Deadlines and waits are anonymous.** A run that reaches its own deadline
is treated as a cancellation: the block is unknown and no message, event or
record says a deadline fired ([E06-01](#e06-01)). The roles' precise
wait-expiry texts, budget, Machine, last answer, stay in the raw output
([C17-01](#c17-01)). While a step runs, the row shows elapsed time for the
block, never for the step, and never the bound of the wait
([O02-03](#o02-03), [O02-04](#o02-04)), so a hang cannot be told from slow
progress.

**8. Remedies that loop, or name no command.** A failed apply always says
"continue it with bootwright apply" ([X16-02](#x16-02)). An unreadable or
contradicted record sends the operator to `status`, which reads the same
record and refuses, or offers no step ([E09-03](#e09-03),
[O03-02](#o03-02)). An unattended destroy over an incomplete apply is told to
take its digest from `plan`, which previews the apply continuation
([X17-06](#x17-06)). Several remedies ask for repairs no command performs:
"restore the target", "restore the context store", "restore credential
custody", a backup restore the spec does not define ([O06-07](#o06-07),
[X03-05](#x03-05), [E07-03](#e07-03)). Others drop the flags the invocation
gave ([E02-03](#e02-03), [E01-04](#e01-04)) or print the literal
`<context>` ([O06-03](#o06-03)).

**9. "Unknown" where the outcome is known.** Deterministic refusals raised
before any effect are coded `lifecycle.unknown`, so every retry first runs a
resolution and reports "Apply unknown" ([C09-06](#c09-06)); `status` says an attempt's outcome "was not recorded"
for attempts that recorded `canceled` or `unknown` for a known cause
([E06-02](#e06-02)); an installation interrupted while its installer still
runs is reported as drift, with the remedy to "restore" it, when the right
step is to wait ([C05-02](#c05-02)).

**10. The result, the progress rows and status hide what stopped.** A settled
`[FAIL]` row erases the step that was running ([O02-01](#o02-01)); pending
rows never say why they did not start ([X11-01](#x11-01)); a destroy paused
for Machines to stop prints a success headline, an error and exit status 1
([X17-04](#x17-04)); an early store or log failure prints a headline with an
empty state and a receipt of four empty values ([O01-04](#o01-04)); an
interrupted run drops the real failures that happened before the interrupt
([O01-02](#o01-02)); a held lock names no holder, and `status` cannot tell a
live apply from one a reboot orphaned ([E11-01](#e11-01),
[X16-06](#x16-06)).

**11. Nothing teaches or pins any of this.** The operator guide keeps its
recovery rules under unrelated headings and has no one place that defines
the states, the exit statuses and the receipt, and no list of codes
([O10-05](#o10-05)). The
CLI goldens of failures render hand-written diagnostics, never the failure
the engine composes, so the text above is pinned by no test
([X13-06](#x13-06)), and no check makes a block's diagnostic name its block
or carry a remedy of its own ([O01-05](#o01-05)).

### 7.3 Twenty journeys

Two lanes reconstructed the full transcript of ten failing journeys each
([X16](#lane-x16), [X17](#lane-x17)). In short:

| Journey | What the operator is told | What is missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A role task fails during a block | "the adapter operation did not complete" | the task, the host, the cause, the right next step |
| The block's target host is unreachable | the same sentence | that the host did not answer, and which host |
| Ctrl-C during an installation | "operation interrupted", the continuation command | nothing; this one reads well |
| Apply repeated soon after that interrupt | "is not what its apply froze", "restore the installation" | that the installer is still running and waiting is the step |
| The SSH session to the controller drops | the interrupt message, to a terminal that is gone | a later `status` cannot say the run was hung up |
| The controller reboots mid-apply | `status` shows the operation running, with a follow command | that nothing is running any more |
| Input edited after a failed apply | an incomplete operation continues from the input it froze; both exits named | nothing |
| A fixed build installed after a failed apply | the contract refusal; destroy under this build or the registering build | where to get the registering build |
| The log root fills up | "a required private operation log could not be maintained", "restore" the directory | that the disk is full |
| The state root fills up | the write, "no space left on device (ENOSPC)", the free-space remedy | nothing |
| A cluster installation wait expires | "an effect has an unresolved outcome" | that a deadline fired, which wait, how long |
| A second apply in another terminal | "context state is held by another mutator" | who holds it and whether it is alive |
| Destroy over an interrupted apply, target unreachable | "cannot prove what these effects left behind" | the exit when the target is gone for good |
| Destroy while Machines run | each Machine and its stop command | nothing; this one reads well |
| Destroy with the hypervisor host down | "still in use", "stop it with machine stop" | that the host did not answer; the stop cannot work; the real exit |
| Destroy with a dead BMC during erase | the endpoint, the Machine, what to restore | the `erase=<machine>:retain` exit its sibling refusals offer |
| Destroy of a Ceph cluster whose hosts stay | not supported, tracked | an exit short of removing the hosts too |
| Destroy without, or with a stale, authorization | the steps, the exact command | under `--yes`, where the digest comes from |
| A removal block fails twice | "the destroy did not complete", repeat | why it failed |
| The operator gives up and deletes the context | "Orphans abandoned true" | the list of what was abandoned |

Six of the twenty are well served. They share one property: the message was
written by the engine for a state the engine names. The other fourteen pass
through a generic sentence on the way from the place that knew the cause to
the operator.

### 7.4 What the real runs add

The two real-run lanes compared, for each attempt that did not succeed, what
Bootwright recorded with what the raw output showed
([Appendix D](#appendix-d-real-run-incidents)). Three patterns: every role
failure reached the operator as the generic sentence; in the three runs that
cut the network on purpose, the role's message said the apply could not
proceed and `Next` said to repeat it, and it was repeated; and sibling blocks
that failed on one shared transient cause produced one identical generic
diagnostic each, with no hint that the cause was common
([O09-07](#o09-07)).

## 8. The meta view: the flows as one explicit state machine

The owner asked for a way for Bootwright to have a meta view of every point
where `apply` and `destroy` can stop, so that each is handled on purpose and
reported with an established message and code, and added the direction:
these operations should be a state machine, so that the possible scenarios
are predictable. This section is the design that answers it. Four independent
designs were written from different angles and scored by three judges against
the code ([8.8](#88-how-the-design-was-chosen)); what follows is the
synthesis, with the alternatives and the open choices named.

### 8.1 What "a state machine" has to mean here

"Predictable" is only worth the work if it can be checked. The design aims at
seven properties, each of which a test can hold:

1. **Every state has a name.** Every condition the flows can be left in,
   durable or in flight, is named and defined by a predicate over the
   records. Today 364 of the 497 conditions the lanes found appear in no
   table.
2. **Every stop is declared.** Every way a verb ends without completing is
   one row with a stable code. Today 1,170 sites share three codes.
3. **Every pair is decided on purpose.** For every state and every event
   that can meet it, a row says what happens. Nothing falls through to a
   generic error.
4. **Every state has a deliberate exit**, or is listed as a terminal the
   owner accepted, with the one command that leaves it.
5. **No remedy loops.** The command a stop names does not lead back to the
   same stop.
6. **What the operator reads is the row, rendered**: what stopped, where,
   why, what state things are in, what to run, kept durably so `status`
   says the same an hour later.
7. **The tables and the code cannot drift apart.** A test compares them in
   both directions, as `TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec` does today for the
   five tables it covers.

### 8.2 What exists to build on

The design adds no new kind of mechanism. Each part generalizes something
the code already does once:

| Already there | Where | What the design does with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One pure decision rule over a verb and six facts | `classify`, `internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/transitions.go` | widens the facts until it decides everything a verb decides |
| Five spec tables held equal to the code | `TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec` | adds tables for the levels that have none |
| A registry of codes held equal to every emission site | `TestDiagnosticCodesMatchOutputSpec`, `test/architecture/diagnostics_test.go` | makes the registry one row per stop, not per family |
| A record that keeps why an observation could not run | the `failure` member of a resolution record | lets every attempt carry it |
| A closed list of adapter endings and of refusal reasons | `internal/adapterprotocol` | makes each ending and each reason a declared stop |
| A harness that kills at every durable write | `internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/kill_harness_test.go` | makes every cut map to a named state |
| A three-valued outcome for a write that may have landed | the registration outcome in `registration.go` | applies it to every such write |
| One helper that computes the exact deletion command | `deletionCommand`, `contradictions.go` | makes it the one "otherwise" exit |

### 8.3 The proposal

**The stop.** A stop is a declared edge of the machine that does not
complete the verb: a refusal, a failed effect, an unproved outcome, a pause,
an interruption. It is declared once, beside the code that raises it, as a
value with these fields:

| Field | Meaning | Closed vocabulary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| code | its stable identity | one per stop |
| level | where the machine stopped | context, operation, removal phase, block, attempt or resolution, adapter run |
| from, event | the states it can fire from and what happened | named states; named events |
| leaves | the state at each level afterwards | named states |
| certainty | what Bootwright knows about effects | none (nothing began), possible (an effect may be partial and a repeat converges), unproved (must be observed first), done-but-owed (the effect is complete, bookkeeping is not) |
| cause | the class of cause | input, environment (with its kind: dns, unreachable, timeout, certificate, credential, proxy, storage, host key), target (absent, foreign, drifted, busy, silent), concurrency, build, records, bound, interrupt, deadline, defect |
| recovery | the class of exit | repeat, fix then repeat, change the input (destroy, then apply), the other verb, wait, authorize, the registering build, abandon the context, none (a defect) |
| exits | the exact commands, in order, with their flags and tokens | commands of the catalog |
| not | the command that will not help | a command |
| otherwise | the last exit when the first may never work | the deletion command with its inventory |
| slots | the names the sentence needs: object, host, block, step, bound | names resolved from Go-owned frozen data |

One firing of a stop is a **stop record**: the code, the slot values, where
it fired (operation, block, attempt, step, task, host), the stop that caused
it when it is a consequence, and the time. It is written with the attempt,
the resolution or the operation it ended, and as an event of the log.

Three consequences follow at once. `status` and `logs` can say why, because
the record is durable. Whether an ending is failed or unknown becomes a
column of the row (its certainty) and stops being inferred from the code
string of an error (`internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/invocation.go:299`).
And a cascade reads as cause then consequence, because each record names its
parent.

**The catalog and the codes.** Every stop is a row of one catalog, published
in the spec and held equal to the declarations by a test. About 400 stops
replace the 1,170 anonymous sites: roughly 110 in the engine, 25 for adapter
endings, 100 declared by roles, and 170 for capability evidence, where one
stop per family of checks carries the failing check as a registered slot
("network active", "disk size"). The three overloaded codes are retired when
the last site has moved.

The format of the code is an owner decision
([section 10](#10-decisions-for-the-owner)). The two serious candidates:

| | A readable name | A number beside a class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Example | `install.network-cutoff`, `runner.task-failed`, `register.index-uncertain` | `BW-6101` with the class `lifecycle.effect-failed` |
| For it | says what it is where it is read; continues the dotted codes and their test; nothing to allocate | short to quote and search; the wording can change under a fixed number |
| Against it | stability depends on discipline; longer | opaque without a lookup; numbers must never be reused |

This report recommends the readable name, with the cause and recovery
classes carried as their own fields in the structured output so that a
script never parses a name.

**Named states and a decision table that decides everything.** Each level
gets its states named, each with the predicate that recognises it from the
records: at the context level, for example, pristine, claimed, registering,
registration possibly landed, registered, removal done with releases owed,
protected with nothing an index accounts for. The crash conditions of
[section 3.3](#33-what-a-cut-leaves-and-who-collects-it) become rows, each
with its exit. Then the facts `classify` reads are widened, one guard at a
time, with what the fifteen early returns around it decide today (a
finalization that is due, an erase relaxation, lost records,
contradictions, the stage selection, the contract proofs, a readable
binding), until the one rule returns every decision and its refusals are
catalog rows. The operation's state is written by one function that reads
the durable block records, in place of five writers.

**The adapter side.** A block's steps are already declared: every capability
freezes its list of groups into the plan, and the role reports each as it
runs. So "where" is known to Go the moment an adapter stops, at no cost. The
design adds:

- every adapter ending is its own stop, and keeps what is thrown away today:
  the exit status or signal, whether the adapter died before it loaded its
  request or after effects began, a deadline as a deadline;
- a safety net for every failure a role did not name: the collection's
  callback reports, on the protocol channel, the last failure nothing
  rescued, as the task's authored name, the step, the host alias and a class
  (task failed, host unreachable, wait exhausted). It never sends a message,
  so no value crosses and `no_log` keeps its guarantee. This alone turns
  "the adapter operation did not complete" into "step boot-installer of
  block os-install-ceph-01 stopped at task 'Wait for the installer to
  answer' on ceph-01: wait exhausted", for every role, before any role is
  converted;
- operator-grade stops are declared: a role names a reason for each stop it
  can diagnose, Go holds the sentence and the exits, and renders the names
  from the frozen request it already has. The 55 named reasons grow toward
  the 306 `assert` and `fail` tasks, role by role, starting with the stops
  the real runs hit;
- environment faults get one closed set of kinds shared by every adapter,
  the one the controller stage already uses for downloads.

**The checks.** These are what make the meta view true and keep it true:

| Check | What it proves | Built on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Closure | no lifecycle diagnostic is built except from a declared stop; a shrinking ledger counts the sites still to move | the code-following analysis of `test/architecture/diagnostics_test.go` |
| Catalog equals spec | the published stops are the implemented ones | the spec-table reader of `transitions_spec_test.go` |
| State-left agreement | the state a stop says it leaves is the one the transition tables give for its certainty | `AttemptTransition`, `ResolutionTransition`, `NextOperationState` |
| Exits | for every stop, each exit it names, decided by `classify` over the state the stop leaves, does not refuse with the same stop; an exit never needs the guard that just failed; a stop whose cause can be permanent names an "otherwise"; `status` is an exit only where status then names a real step | the pure `classify` |
| Accepted terminals | the set of states whose only exit is abandoning the context equals a short table in the spec | the same model |
| Crash prefixes, with total accounting | at every kill point, every directory, claim, reservation and binding is explained by a named state, and the next verb converges or raises a declared stop | the kill harness |
| A golden per stop, and journey goldens | what the operator reads for each stop is pinned, through the real engine, in `apply`, `status`, `logs` and `explain` | the CLI golden machinery |
| Role reasons | every reason a role emits is declared and maps to a stop; task names are static | the collection's role-boundary tests |
| Store transition guard | the store refuses a block, attempt or resolution write the block table does not admit | the operation store |

### 8.4 What the operator would read

The same failed apply as in [section 7.1](#71-a-failed-apply-as-it-reads-today),
taken from one of the real runs that cut a Machine's network on purpose, as
it would read (an illustration; names and layout are for the slices to
settle):

```text
  ! Apply failed: 1 step stopped; repeating apply will not help

  Result
  Substrates
    [DONE] realize the libvirt host of lab-libvirt on controller
  Machines
    [DONE] realize the virtual machine nv-bond and its emulated BMC
    [FAIL] install the operating system of nv-bond · stopped while converging the network
    [PENDING] install the operating system of nv-vlan · waits for nothing; not started after the stop

  Stopped  install.network-cutoff
    What     the declared network of Machine nv-bond made 192.0.2.10 unreachable
             from Machine controller, and the change was rolled back
    Where    block os-install-nv-bond · attempt 2 · step converge-network ·
             task "Stop at a declared network that cut the controller off"
    Why      input: this network cannot be applied without cutting the
             controller off; the same stop as attempt 1
    Now      block failed, nothing left half-applied · operation failed
    Next     1. bootwright destroy --context nv-cutoff
             2. correct the network of Machine/nv-bond
             3. bootwright apply --context nv-cutoff
    Not      bootwright apply --context nv-cutoff stops the same way
    Read     bootwright logs --context nv-cutoff --block os-install-nv-bond --attempt 2 --raw
    Explain  bootwright explain install.network-cutoff

operation: op-<id>
verb: apply
state: failed
next: destroy
stop: install.network-cutoff
```

`bootwright status` an hour later prints the same block from the durable
record, with when it happened and whether a command is running now.
`bootwright explain <code>` prints the catalog row: what the stop means, the
states it leaves, whether repeating helps, its exits. The operator guide's
reference of stops is generated from the catalog.

### 8.5 How far to take the machine

There are three depths, and the choice between the second and the third is
the one place where this report is more cautious than a literal reading of
"make it a state machine".

| Depth | What changes | What it gives | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Named and reported | stops declared, persisted and rendered; the adapter safety net; the closure check | properties 2 and 6: the owner's complaint is answered | low: no control flow changes |
| 2. Decided by tables | named states with predicates; the widened decision rule; one writer of the operation state; the exit, terminal and crash-prefix checks; the store guard | properties 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7: every scenario is a row, and tests hold rows and code equal | moderate: the decision code is reshaped, guard by guard, each under the existing tests |
| 3. Executed from tables | the engine changes state only by looking up a declared row; registration, an attempt and the completion of a removal run as step lists under one generic runner | drift between table and code becomes impossible by construction | high: it rewrites the registration and completion code whose crash behavior the kill harness proves today |

The recommendation is depth 2, reached through depth 1, and depth 3 as a
later decision. The reason is specific: the three judges, reading the code,
each ranked the design that rewrites the executor last, because the
registration and completion sequences span separate transactions with
deliberate orderings (the claim before the evidence, the binding outside the
store lock, the re-proof of the exact claim list), and a generic runner with
undo would be new recovery behavior over code that today passes a kill at
every write. Depth 2 gives the predictability the owner asked for: the
scenarios are enumerable from the declared tables and the tests fail when
the code and the tables disagree. Depth 3 changes how that agreement is
enforced, not what is known. If the checks of depth 2 keep finding drift,
that is the evidence for depth 3.

### 8.6 Dead ends in the machine

Once exits are checked, a dead end is a test failure or a row of the
accepted-terminals table. The audit's dead ends
([section 6](#6-dead-ends-and-loose-ends)) sort into three treatments:

- **An exit exists and is not named.** The stop gains its "otherwise": the
  deletion command with the list of what it abandons. This covers a target
  that is gone or silent, lost and contradicted records, bounds that never
  retire. No behavior changes; the operator is told.
- **The remedy loops or names no command.** The exit check rejects it until
  it is replaced: a failed apply whose `Next` repeats the failure, `status`
  as the remedy for a record `status` cannot read, a Machine stop as the
  exit for a hypervisor that does not answer, "restore" with nothing to
  restore from.
- **A narrower exit would need new behavior.** A scoped acknowledgement for
  one target that is gone for good, keeping the build that registered an
  operation, letting a destroy supersede an incomplete removal after a build
  update. Each changes policy and is an owner decision; until it is taken
  the state is an accepted terminal, listed, with its deletion exit. The
  catalog makes each one a single new row when the decision lands.

### 8.7 What this does not solve

- Effects on remote hosts keep running after a local kill or deadline. The
  machine can name the state ("an effect may still be progressing") and
  require an observation; it cannot stop the work or say how long to wait.
- A target that is gone still blocks its own removal by policy. The design
  makes that legible and, if the owner decides so, narrower. It does not
  make a dead host answer.
- A wrong postcondition check is still a wrong check, now with a precise
  code. The checks prove the rows and the code agree, not that each
  capability's predicate is right.
- About 400 declarations have to be written and classified once. A wrong
  class yields a confidently wrong `Next`; the golden per stop is the review
  that catches it.

### 8.8 How the design was chosen

Four designers each took one angle and argued it without hedging: a registry
of stops over today's control flow; a fully declared hierarchical machine
with one writer and a model checker; procedures as declared step lists with
derived crash states; and the operator's stop report first. Three judges
scored them from 1 to 5 on seven criteria, one as the maintainer of the
engine, one as the operator running at night, one as the safety and
architecture reviewer, each checking feasibility claims in the code.

| Design | Engine judge | Operator judge | Safety judge | Strongest idea carried over |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Registry of stops | 29 | 28 | 29 | the three bindings: closure, state-left agreement, the exit check through `classify` |
| Stop report first | 27 | 28 | 26 | the report (what, where, why, now, next, not), "same stop as attempt 1", one `Next` from the first stop |
| Step procedures | 25 | 25 | 24 | crash prefixes with total accounting; the store transition guard |
| Declared machine, one writer | 23 | 22 | 22 | the widened decision facts; the permanence rule; the closed terminals table |

All three judges proposed the same synthesis: the registry as the spine,
delivered in the stop report's order, moving toward the declared machine by
widening the decision rule, without the single writer or the step runner.
Things the judges rejected and this report therefore does not propose: free
task or vendor text crossing the adapter channel; automatic undo; a scoped
abandonment that makes the evidence read pristine; and changing an
undeclared adapter failure from failed to unknown by default. The last two
and four more are questions only the owner can settle; they are listed in
[section 10](#10-decisions-for-the-owner).

## 9. Plan

The plan has seven workstreams. It is a proposal: it authorizes nothing, and
each slice needs the owner's go-ahead and its own milestone items before any
code changes. Sizes are S (about a day), M (a few days), L (one to two
weeks) and XL (a program of its own, delivered capability by capability).

### 9.1 Order

```text
now          W6.1 the Secret-binding release (one small fix, regression test first)
first        W1.1 keep the cause  ->  W1.2 causes on their blocks  ->  W1.3 adapter endings
             ->  W1.4 the safety net for role failures
             (these four answer the owner's complaint without converting a single role)
then         W1.5 remedies that work     W6 the other unsafe points, in parallel
next         W2.1 stops, catalog, codes, explain  ->  W2.2 outcome from certainty
             W3.1 named states  ->  W4.1 exit check  ->  W4.2 crash prefixes
after        W3.2 the widened decision rule, guard by guard     W3.3 one writer
long tail    W2.3 role stops and W2.4 evidence stops, per capability, by how often
             real runs hit them: installation, Ceph hosts and cluster, OpenShift
             installation, then the rest
as decided   W5 deliberate exits for dead ends (each waits for a decision of
             section 10)
alongside    W7 prevention and documentation
```

### 9.2 W1: say why

Purpose: after any stop, the operator can read what failed, where and why,
at once and an hour later. No control flow changes in this workstream.

| Slice | What it delivers | Closes | Size | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

W1.1 changes two record formats by adding an optional member, and W1.4
changes the adapter protocol; under the development policy each is a
breaking change for operations in flight and says so in its commit.
