stored. Attempt.Failure is filled only for resolutions, and the attempt jsonl
records only "outcome failed", so `status` cannot later say why a block
failed. Effects on remote hosts after cancellation are already tracked as
B573.

Strengths to keep:

- Process-tree lifetime is engineered end to end. The adapter is forked from a
  locked OS thread with Pdeathsig, the supervisor is a subreaper that kills
  session-isolated workers, and the playbook child arms its own SIGUSR2
  parent-death guard. The runner signals the supervisor before the group kill.
  Native tests back each step (ansible-worker-session-isolation.md).
- Every adapter ending is one value of a closed enum (adapterprotocol.Kind),
  with explicit precedence rules between a failed exit and records read after
  it, and a bounded drain. This is the nucleus of an explicit state machine.
- The job lock plus holder lock distinguishes a live sibling, a live
  same-context run and leftover descendants. The refusals name context,
  description, operation, Machine or lock path, and sweeps decide on held
  handles without following links.
- Strict canonical, bounded decoding with closed refusal reasons, the closed
  `detail` grammar and opt-in `nativeError` give a safe way to carry causes.
  Named refusals already produce actionable, object-naming diagnostics.
- Hygiene: lent material is 0600 under /run and cleared from memory, there is
  a per-job ssh_config with ControlMaster=no and ControlPersist=no, extra-vars
  are written as unsafe data, and output is unbuffered (-u) so the transcript is
  live.

#### Lane E11

**Context store, locks, lease, transactions and the deletion guard**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The store's locking is simple and
robust at the kernel level: two flock locks (host-wide root lock on the root
inode, per-context lease on the context directory), every descriptor opened
O_CLOEXEC through openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH, so a dead holder never leaves a
stale lock and nothing is ever taken over. Mutators wait up to one minute for
the root lock; a lease and every reader refuse at once. Every record
publication stages beside its target, proves the destination right before one
rename, and distinguishes not-committed, committed and unknown outcomes; the
lifecycle engine treats a raised evidence publication as possibly landed.
Recorded directory identity compares inode plus same-filesystem-as-parent and
never a recorded device, so btrfs reboots are safe; incarnation adds birth
time or inode generation. Deletion is a durable two-phase walk (mark Deleting,
drop controller claims, remove tree, remove logs, drop registry entry) whose
retry resumes. Where it is thin: (1) a busy lock says nothing about who holds
it, whether it is the root lock or this context's lease, or whether the holder
is alive, and status probes no liveness, so a stopped or hung holder is
indistinguishable from a running one or an interrupted one; (2) a failed log
write drops the kernel's answer and tells the operator to 'restore' the log
tree; (3) store-wide verification turns one context's damage into a refusal of
every context, and the exits name a whole-store restore no command performs
and no procedure or test defines; (4) an orphan-acknowledged deletion reports
only 'Orphans abandoned: true' and points at status/diff, which stop working
once the context is gone, and with --yes the plan is never printed; (5)
several low-level refusals (unlink failure, non-EWOULDBLOCK flock error,
evidence read error) use texts that name no entry or misname the cause.

Strengths to keep:

- Locks cannot go stale on death: both locks are flock on descriptors opened
  O_CLOEXEC through openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH (nativefs/open_linux.go:67), and
  UnlockAndClose unlocks before closing so a forked child cannot keep a lock;
  nothing ever takes a lock over.
- Every record publication stages beside its target, proves the destination
  right before a single rename and classifies not-committed / committed /
  unknown (publication_linux_amd64.go:47-96), and the engine treats a raised
  evidence publication as possibly landed.
- Recorded directory identity is inode plus same-device-as-parent and never a
  recorded st_dev, so btrfs anonymous device renumbering after reboot does not
  refuse the store (kernel/directory_linux_amd64.go:104), and incarnation adds
  birth time or inode generation against inode reuse.
- Deletion is durable and resumable: mark Deleting under the lease and
  evidence re-proof, then remove through held, re-verified handles, preserving
  identifying entries until last; a repeat purge resumes from any point.
- Most damage refusals name the context, the entry relative to the state root,
  the kernel's answer and a specific exit (contextDamage,
  deletionEntryRemediation, evidenceRemediation).

#### Lane E12

**Secrets during a lifecycle run: bindings, keyring, custody and lent
material**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The Secret layer is the strongest
part of the lifecycle I have seen. Bindings pin whole immutable versions.
Every publication is one authenticated metadata swap: parts and seals are
written first, the selector is replaced last, and orphan artifacts are
collected by the next session. Material is cleared on every path. A reopen
that fails is split into "lost" (keyring corrupt or undecryptable, or a
listing that no longer names the binding) and "reported as it failed", and the
lost-binding diagnostic names the operation, its state, the binding, why it is
lost and every owned object. It is thin in three places. 1. The lost-binding
verdict hangs on the code secret.store.corrupt, and that code is keyring-wide.
The session open checks the whole keyring. One stray file, an unrelated
Secret's missing part or an unsupported layout fails every session, so every
binding is declared lost. The only offered exits are a restore or `context
delete --purge --allow-orphans`, even when deleting a stray file would have
fixed it. 2. A keyring that stays unusable after a removal is recorded done
cannot finish. The Release and Withdraw calls fail on every repeat, while the
remedy says to repeat destroy. 3. Diagnostics raised inside the keyring carry
no object: no Secret, version, binding or file path. The default remedies for
key-unavailable ("unlock session") and for the seal limit ("reduce the
material") do not fit the local keyring. Bounded consumers, holds against
renewal and the registration window are handled deliberately and are well
tested. `secret delete` is the one mutation that bypasses holds.

Strengths to keep:

- Bindings pin whole immutable versions with an equality check against the
  stored version (mutations.go Bind and equalVersion), and are never re-bound
  from current declarations. A continuation or removal presents exactly the
  material that created its effects.
- Single-swap publication: parts, seals and a fresh key are written
  exclusively first, the authenticated selector is replaced last, and leftovers
  are collected by the next session. A crash at any point leaves either the old
  or the new keyring, never a mix.
- The lost-binding diagnostic names the operation, its state, the binding, the
  reason and every owned object, and re-reads the context so a binding released
  since the decision reports that change (frozenbinding.go lostBinding).
- Holds read before any prompt and re-proved under the lease, with an explicit
  unnamed-binding window for an apply still registering. Bounded consumers
  publish nothing. Material is cleared on every path, a cancellation included.
- Produced-material capture failure is deliberately recorded unknown rather
  than failed, so a destroy cannot delete the only copy without first observing
  and recapturing (produced.go capturedAttempt).

#### Lane E13

**The controller stage: prerequisites, runtime, bundle, host binding and
client tools**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The controller stage is the most
carefully built part of the lifecycle I read. Before every registration,
`approvedRuntime` checks the setup record (foreign or interrupted), the
receipt and the published runtime. A missing runtime is rebuilt from the wheel
cache with no network, and the stage refuses with `controller install` only
when a wheel is missing. A continuation also re-checks the host binding and
the Python/Ansible closure. The tool stage records its intent (preparation
plus retained sources) before any dnf or download. dnf runs under a
non-waiting `controller/install/lock` with presence read again under the lock.
A failed install after it started is recorded as unknown. The Ansible protocol
separates "never authorized" (failed) from "acknowledgement may have been
delivered" (unknown), and Go maps the acquisition classes (dns, proxy,
timeout, certificate, ...) to diagnostics that name the source host and the
command that settles it. The stage's removal is a no-op that publishes
retained evidence, so destroy never depends on publishers. The thin spots are
in output and in a few remedies. First, about 15 Go-side adapter failures
share one correction, "Preserve the controller state and restore the qualified
controller execution environment", including operator-fixable ones such as
/var/tmp being too small or a lent trust anchor that is not a certificate.
Second, any Python refusal outside the classified set (bundle ownership or
replacement, file size, publication bounds) emits no record and no warning:
the operator gets "Ansible did not complete the authorized dependency
operation" and the cause exists nowhere. Third, during a destroy, an
executable the removal cannot locate is refused with "run bootwright apply
--stage controller", which the transition table refuses while that destroy is
incomplete. Finally, the dnf install deadline and the timeout of a mirror
anchor are reported as configuration problems.

Strengths to keep:

- Intent before effect: the stage records the exact dnf requirements and tool
  sources (RetainDependencies + Prepare) before dnf or any download, and the
  adapter must announce exactly those sources before Go acknowledges
  (capability.go:395-405, protocol.go validPreparation).
- The authorized/unauthorized split in protocolRun.unauthorized/outcome
  separates 'never acknowledged, nothing done' (failed) from 'acknowledgement
  may have been delivered' (unknown), counting an EPIPE as proof of
  non-delivery; this is the precise outcome rule every adapter should share.
- Closed refusal classes from Python (dns, certificate, proxy, timeout, ...)
  are mapped in Go to messages that name the source host and the tool area,
  never carrying exception text (refusals.go, controller_files.py classify).
- Readiness equals completion: Observe, Apply and settled all judge by rpm
  presence and area presence, so a repeated apply contacts no publisher and an
  interrupted stage is completed by repetition (seal-on-replay).
- The runtime is located once per operation, rebuilt offline from cached
  wheels, and its closure is frozen into the operation, so a continuation can
  never run under a different Ansible/Python without an explicit refusal naming
  the build.

#### Lane E14

**Composition root: capability binding and error translation for
reconciliation**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The composition root binds
capabilities through a closed, ordered resolver keyed on (kind,
implementation). Resolve returns false for a binding whose capability is nil,
so a block frozen against an implementation this build lacks is refused rather
than run against another one. The playbook map is closed too: an unbound
implementation/operation pair refuses before any process starts. Contract
fingerprints come from one embedded manifest that a golden test pins, and
every continuation proves them before it reads anything. That part is strong
and fails closed. Error translation is where the slice is thin. The root adds
no translation of its own. Three kinds of failure lose the cause because the
composition swallows a build-integrity error or a non-diagnostic error: - A
composition failure (no embedded runtime lock, or a nil port in
Service.configured) shows up as "bootwright apply is not implemented" with a
help remedy. - If the contract manifest fails to decode, the map is nil. Every
apply then refuses each block with "use the executable that registered the
operation", even when no operation exists. - A plain Go error from the service
reaches the runner's last branch, "application service returned an unsupported
result" (runtime.internal, exit 255). Inside a block it becomes "the block X
stopped on a failure that escaped a typed boundary". Both drop the real cause
and blame a Bootwright defect. Status readiness discards secret and media read
errors, so status can look healthier than it is. Resolve failures that the
continuation proof has already settled return a generic "install the
executable that registered this operation" remedy that names no version,
unlike the proveExecution remedy, which does. Most of these paths need a build
defect or an unusual store error, so the severities are Low to Medium. Still,
each is a stop with no specific code and no cause, which is exactly what the
meta view needs to enumerate.

Strengths to keep:

- The capability resolver is closed and keyed on (kind, implementation), and
  Resolve refuses a nil capability. A block frozen against one implementation
  never runs against another implementation of the same kind
  (wiring_reconciliation.go:131-138).
- The playbook map is closed and owned by composition: desired state never
  names a playbook, and an unbound pair refuses before any process starts.
- Execution contracts come from one embedded manifest pinned by a golden test
  that make build runs, and every continuation proves them before reading
  records (spec 'Dependency safety during recovery').
- proveExecution gives a version-named, take-back-aware remedy for a contract
  or implementation miss on continuation (other_build.go:79-85). This model is
  worth generalizing to every Resolve-miss site.
- The Capability port makes Removal, Quiescent and ObserveRemoval mandatory
  methods, so no capability can silently opt out of the removal gates
  (contracts.go:198-227).

#### Lane G01

**Plan-time, freeze-time and thaw-time refusals of the capability requests**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Most of the roughly 218 sites are
plan-time derivation refusals: Ceph catalog checks, installation and Kickstart
derivation, artifact-server and agent-install selection. They fire before
registration, so the operator edits the input and repeats. Most name the
object and the field (for example the CephPool, CephSMBResource and
Machine/\<name> forms). The shared freeze and thaw functions are strict: the
version is read before the shape, the shape is decoded closed, and the bytes
are proved canonical. Thaw-time decode refusals are well contained by
lifecycle. proveExecution reads every frozen request through its capability
before a continuation or removal plan is presented. It rewrites the refusal so
that it names the block and the registering build (removal_plan.go
unreadable). So the many empty or "plan the installation again" remedies
inside the Decode* validators rarely reach the operator there. The lane is
weakest after registration, at attempt time, where a capability checks bound
Secret material or another block's proof. Three such checks send the operator
to rebind or reset a Secret and "apply again": the FIPS Ceph cluster key, the
Ceph SMB password and the FIPS agent-installation SSH key. A continuation
reuses the bound version, so the advice cannot work, and the real exit is
destroy. The installation capability already says so for the same class of
problem. The dependency-proof refusals (host key, DVD tree, data-disk volume,
discovered root) name no Machine or profile. They use one sentence for several
causes and point to "restore" remedies that no command performs. The
disk-refinement gate after `machine discover` names neither the object nor the
field. Finally, the controller-prerequisites block destroys nothing, yet its
strict decode and its contract equality gate every continuation and removal.
Its package table lives outside the contract guard's paths.

Strengths to keep:

- reconciliation.ThawVersion reads the version before the shape, decodes
  closed and proves the bytes canonical (frozen.go:34-55). A changed shape
  cannot carry an old digest, and an unknown version is named when it is a
  readable segment.
- proveExecution reads every frozen request through its capability before a
  continuation or removal is presented, and rewrites the refusal so it names the
  block and the registering build (other_build.go:20-58,
  removal_plan.go:122-136). This contains the dozens of weakly worded Decode*
  validators.
- The installation key refusals are the model to copy: fipsKey,
  deliveredKeyMatches, generatedHostKeyType and fipsNotEnabled name the Machine,
  the Secret, the key type, 'nothing was published or booted', and destroy as
  the exit, with the reason (key_policy.go:53-58).
- Dependency proofs read only the original apply lineage's durable records
  (ApplyProved), never live observations or ambient known_hosts, and re-validate
  each against its owner's frozen request and digest (dependency_proof.go,
  package_tree_proof.go, evidence.go:161-218).
- Plan-time Ceph resource refusals name the object and the field and give a
  concrete edit (resources.go, service_unit.go:231-249, smb_materials.go:21).

#### Lane G02

**Small roles and helper utilities the first round did not cite**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Most of this lane follows one pattern
that works well. A hidden native call runs with `failed_when: false`, then a
`refused` record carries a closed reason (with `module-failure` as the
fallback detail), then a terminal `fail` runs, and the completed record comes
only from proved evidence. The Ceph consumer, image and SMB roles, the
controller prerequisites (through controller_tool's `name()`), and the
disk-discovery runtime (a phase and a code mapped to fixed operator text) all
do this. The low-level helpers are careful about durability.
registry_auth.lent checks the file it lends and removes it. libvirt_nm_carrier
records a pending reload in the file itself, so a cut reload converges on the
next apply. redfish_remote_ca re-reads the slot inventory before and after
every trust write, so a lost reply converges on retry. The discovery SSH
custody is staged and renamed, and a staged leftover is collected. The
disk-discovery worker fails closed into an inert loop that prints a fixed
console line. Where it is thin: - **Administrator credential.** The roles
break the pattern: the module fails without `failed_when: false`, under
`no_log`, with no reason vocabulary. Every cause becomes the generic adapter
failure, and the Go remedy written for this flow can never be reached. -
**Package transaction.** A DNF transaction cut part way leaves an inventory
that the frozen decision refuses on every repeat apply (`package-drift`). The
remedy does not say that only destroy and a fresh apply leave this state. -
**Generic fallbacks.** Several helpers raise raw OSError or unmapped
ValueError text. These land in generic fallbacks ("could not be proved", "a
bounded discovery contract was refused") with no path and no cause. -
**Unknown answers.** machine_power_read promises that a controller which does
not answer leaves only its own machine unknown. In fact, any templating,
assert or dispatch failure for one target fails the whole reading. - **Trust
anchor ownership.** The SecurityService helper treats any slot holding the
same authority as its own, whoever installed it. A trust-unproved refusal is
silently accepted on the next attempt.

Strengths to keep:

- The hidden-call pattern (failed_when: false, then a `refused` record with a
  closed reason and a module-failure fallback, then a terminal fail, with
  `completed` only from evidence) in the storage_ceph_* roles gives Go a reason
  even when the module crashes, and keeps vendor text out.
- Retry convergence through read-back: redfish_remote_ca re-reads slots before
  and after each write, containercluster_admin_credentials skips a patch already
  applied, node placement patches only what is missing with uid and labels
  test-pinned, and the monitoring template settles a lost reply by exact
  read-back.
- libvirt_nm_carrier records a pending reload inside the owned file itself, so
  a cut reload is visible to observation and repaired by the next apply with no
  extra state file.
- The disk-discovery runtime's REFUSALS, FAILURES and PHASES tables give one
  operator sentence per phase and code. They are the closest thing in this lane
  to a registered stop catalog, with remedies such as reading the console phase
  for inventory-timeout.
- Durable custody staging: disk_discovery_ssh stages keys in a hidden
  directory and renames it, reaps orphan stages on the next run, and refuses
  foreign material. registry_auth.lent checks the lent file both before and
  after the native client holds it.

#### Lane O01

**Lifecycle results, receipt and diagnostics rendering, human and structured**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** When apply or destroy ends after
registration, the CLI writes the lifecycle result to standard output: a
headline, Result rows in frozen plan order by stage, Logs and Follow, a Next
command, then the four-line receipt. Only after that does it write every
diagnostic to standard error, both warnings and errors (results.go:51-54). In
a terminal the cause therefore appears below the receipt. The diagnostic has
no block field, so it is linked to its row only when it carries an object
identity or names its block in its remedy text (the adapter-failure remedy
does). The renderer sorts all diagnostics by source, then code, then object,
then message (output.go:192, diagnostics.Compare). The order is not by block,
by time or by severity, so with several failed blocks the first cause cannot
be told apart. The terminal "the apply did not complete" also lands wherever
its message sorts alphabetically. Result rows carry the state and the attempt
outcome but never the cause. JSON carries more than text: attempts per block
and the per-block unresolved {reason, remedy}, which the human result drops.
Strong points: one shared renderer escapes everything once, the receipt is
stable, Next names the exact command with --context, an interrupted registered
operation still prints its result and receipt, and a stdout write failure
never falls back to stderr. Thin points: the ordering rule conflicts with the
destroy resolution remedy, which says to read "the result's last diagnostic".
An interrupt drops genuine earlier failures. A destroy paused at its stop
boundary shows a check-mark headline but exits 1. A result registered but not
finished renders an empty receipt. The default remedy keeps a literal
\<context> when the context came from the current-context setting. The goldens
pin a shape (no outcome suffix, a single terminal diagnostic) that production
no longer emits.

Strengths to keep:

- One display boundary escapes every untrusted value exactly once
  (escapeDiagnostics, escapeDisplayLine), and the receipt is written by one
  function with fixed labels and order.
- An executed failure keeps its result, Logs, Follow, exact Next command (with
  --context and bound --authorize tokens) and receipt on stdout, and keeps
  diagnostics on stderr. The JSON envelope carries the same membership plus
  logs.
- The Next command and the receipt token come from one rule (nextAction and
  continuationCommand), shared with plan and status.
- An interrupted registered operation still prints its result and receipt and
  names the continuing command as the interrupt's remedy.
- A stdout write failure never falls back to stderr (lifecycleOutputFailure).

#### Lane O02

**Progress presentation when a step fails, hangs or is cancelled**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The progress presenter is careful
about terminal mechanics. Rows are bounded to the width and redrawn in place,
outcomes are held back to plan order, echo is held while rows are drawn, and
the clock and width are injected. It never claims an outcome it did not
observe. Its weakness is what it says while a step fails or stalls. The engine
settles every lifecycle row with Status set to the block state and an empty
Detail (attempts.go:135). settle() then overwrites the row's last sub-step
with that empty detail. So a [FAIL] or [UNKNOWN] row names neither the
presentation group that was running nor any reason. On a terminal, the running
row that named the group has already been overwritten, so the 'where'
disappears from the screen. The real logs show no adapter group ever settled
'failed' (3,334 running and 3,283 ok records, no failed). The last running
group is therefore the only pointer to where a failure happened, and it is
dropped. While a step runs, the heartbeat shows the time since the step
started, not since the current sub-step began. On a terminal, a byte measure
fully replaces the heartbeat, with no staleness bound. No wait names its
budget, except the physical-erase wait note. After a failure, the scheduler
admits nothing new and drains the blocks in flight. After a first interrupt,
it waits for the in-flight blocks to record their outcomes. In both cases the
presenter shows nothing about this state. After an interrupt every row freezes
silently, because report() drops events on a cancelled context. The [CANCELED]
token can never appear for a lifecycle block, because a cancelled attempt maps
to the unknown state.

Strengths to keep:

- The presenter never claims an unobserved outcome. Only durable done events
  advance the meter, and a cancelled step writes nothing. This honesty has to
  stay in any redesign.
- Terminal mechanics are robust and tested: rows are bounded to the width, the
  block height is exact, outcomes are held back in plan order, echo is held
  while rows are drawn, and the clock and width are injected
  (terminal-progress-redraw.md documents each defect it fixed).
- The byte meter shows only a rate the presenter observed on its own clock,
  after a 10s warmup, and logs the measure at bounded intervals, so an adapter's
  claim of speed is never shown.
- A resolution that leaves the block failed keeps one row running into the
  retry with an explicit sub-step ('the effect is unfinished; retrying it').
  This is a good model for naming in-flight transitions.
- The physical-erase GroupNote ('waiting for the erase worker at \<addr>, no
  answer for N min (\<reason>)') names the target, the silence and the last error
  inside a closed grammar. Every wait could reuse this pattern.

#### Lane O03

**status as the "what happened and what now" command**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Status is a careful, probe-free read
of durable records. Its strong side is unproved blocks. For each unknown or
running block, unresolvedOf rebuilds a Reason and Remedy from the last
resolution: the stored ObservationFailure, the capability's own Unresolved or
Drifted text, or the command that observes the block. The Next steps list is
filtered, so status does not offer a verb whose re-proof (input drift, build
contracts, closure, setup, binding) would refuse. The weak side is failed
blocks, the most common failure class. The durable attempt record cannot hold
a failure diagnostic: validFailure admits one only on a resolution. The
attempt log keeps only `outcome failed`. So after a failed apply or destroy,
status shows `[FAIL] <description>` and nothing else: no cause, no time
(Started/Updated are recorded but not shown), and in human text no attempt
count. The adapter's clear message survives only in the root-owned raw
.output. Where status's own filtering drops the continuation, it also drops
the refusal's message and remedy. When the records contradict themselves, the
refusals of both verbs send the operator to status, and status lists the
contradiction with an empty Next steps: a remedy loop. Status also cannot tell
an invocation running now from one that was interrupted. It tells a running
block's operator that the outcome 'was not recorded' and to run apply, which
then refuses on the lease. Status fails outright, and shows none of the
lifecycle, when the selected input does not compile (for example under a new
build) or when any record read fails. Some of its own refusals name 'restore
the context store' as the only remedy.

Strengths to keep:

- unresolvedOf/explain gives an unknown block a specific Reason and Remedy
  from the last resolution's recorded ObservationFailure or the capability's own
  Unresolved/Drifted text, naming the subject and host (cli-status-unresolved
  golden). This is the model a failed block should follow.
- offered() and continuation() re-run the same re-proofs the verbs run, so
  status never offers a verb those records would refuse (setup, binding,
  closure, contracts, input drift).
- Status is strictly probe-free and lock-safe: shared reads, no writes, and a
  Live section that lists each running block's newest output file and its size
  from records alone.
- The realization fold (appliedStatus/removedStatus/replacedRemovals) reports
  the state that needs action first, never the most favorable one, across
  removal lineages.
- Recorded failure text is bounded and made valid UTF-8 (bounded()), and every
  displayed field is escaped (escapeDisplayLine), so storing more diagnostics is
  safe to add.

#### Lane O04

**logs as the "why" command: content, access and retention**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The log layer is careful about its
own integrity. Records are bounded and closed-decoded, a write failure latches
and stops the run, truncation is stated explicitly, files are created
exclusively without following links, retained output is published within a
second, and `bootwright logs` reads under short shared locks and escapes
everything it prints. It is weak as the operator's "why" command. The event
grammar records only that something happened: the `outcome` event holds a
single word, a group event's status is only ever `running` or `ok` (the group
that failed stays `running`), and the operation log holds nothing but one
`opened` per invocation. The diagnostic the operator saw on standard error for
a failed effect attempt is not stored anywhere durable. The record validator
allows a `failure` only on an unknown resolution, so `status` cannot show it
later either. The cause therefore lives only in the raw
`attempt-NNNNNN.output`, which is root-only and up to 4 MiB, is dumped whole
by `logs --raw`, and is full of Ansible `FAILED - RETRYING` polling lines
(2,656 of them in 215 of 1,663 outputs). The real cause line (`[ERROR]: Task
failed` / `fatal:`) usually sits near the end. For the Ceph family it is
worse: the adapter publishes the reason through the no_log result protocol,
the raw output says only "the run names its reason", and the reason survives
in neither file. Resolutions are better than effect attempts:
`observation-failed` and `unresolved` events and `Attempt.failure` keep code
and message. Retention is reasonable in size (64 operations, 128 MiB; the
largest sampled operation was about 1.3 MB), but `context delete --purge` and
`context init` erase the log evidence, and the runtime.log fault drops its
underlying error.

Strengths to keep:

- Resolutions already persist their cause: `observation-failed` events carry
  `code: message` and Attempt.failure stores code, message and remedy bounded
  and validated. This is the mechanism to generalize to effect attempts.
- Log integrity is careful: exclusive creation under verified handles, closed
  decoding of every record, sticky write failure with no gap-crossing appends,
  explicit truncation markers, and the attempt log's group-limit tail
  reservation.
- Retained output is published within a second (8 KiB batch or 1 s timer,
  retried while the run lasts), so a wedged run is readable while it is still in
  flight.
- `bootwright logs` never makes another command fail: shared lock without
  waiting, bytes read after release, busy polls skipped, a bounded 60-poll
  refusal, and a detached-executor warning that names the continuing verb.
- Every byte shown in text mode passes the display escaper, and the exact
  bytes leave only through the structured export.

#### Lane O05

**Diagnostic taxonomy: code overload and a class census**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The diagnostic type is a flat record:
severity, code, message, source, object, field, remediation. A refusal is a
*Failure holding a list of them. Strong points: the registry test follows
codes through constants, variables, parameters and methods, so no code goes
undocumented, and every registered error code has a default remedy that is
filled with the resolved context name. A block cause that carries no
diagnostic becomes runtime.internal without leaking its text. Three codes
carry 1,133 literal sites, and the code tells the operator almost nothing
about what happened or what state is left. lifecycle.state covers at least ten
classes whose exits differ: - repeat apply; - observe, then repeat; - destroy
and re-apply; - use the build that registered the operation; - restore the
input revision; - restore the context store; - fix a host prerequisite; -
report a Bootwright defect. The code is also load-bearing in an inconsistent
way. AttemptOutcome maps any diagnostic other than lifecycle.unknown to a
failed block. MutateBlock instead sets the outcome to unknown on every
evidence-check refusal, and about 220 of those carry lifecycle.state. Ceph
uses lifecycle.unknown for the same class. So the code neither predicts the
block state nor matches the registry meaning. The diagnostics that explain a
block's failure are not durable. An attempt record may not carry a failure:
the validator allows one only on an observed unknown resolution. The attempt
log holds only `outcome failed` and the raw output. Once stderr is gone,
status and logs cannot say why a failed block failed. Block causes carry no
block identity field and are re-sorted by code and message before printing. In
a multi-block failure the operator cannot pair a cause with its [FAIL] row.
The adapter-failure remedy names a root-only file path rather than `bootwright
logs --raw --block`.

Strengths to keep:

- TestDiagnosticCodesMatchOutputSpec follows codes through constants,
  variables, parameters, method sets and function values, and fails on any write
  it cannot follow, so the registry cannot drift from emissions.
- Every registered error code has a tested default remedy, filled with the
  invoking context's name (WithRemediationFor,
  TestEveryErrorCodeHasADefaultRemediation).
- Undiagnosed block causes become runtime.internal naming the block, never
  echoing raw store text, and default to the conservative unknown outcome
  (scheduler.reported, AttemptOutcome).
- Ceph and libvirt named refusals are closed maps (reason to diagnostic) with
  specific, often excellent remedies, and the adapter detail and native
  coordinate are appended in bounded form (refusalDetail, refusalNative).
- Resolution failures are recorded durably (ObservationFailure) and status
  re-reports them, the right pattern to extend to attempts.

#### Lane O06

**Remedies: every "Next" an operator is given in the lifecycle area**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The lifecycle engine writes its own
remedies with care. contextCommand always binds `--context` to the resolved
context. A continuation carries every frozen token bound to its digest. A
failed destroy names the replacement. An unknown apply names both the
resolution and the take-back. status offers only the verbs its records would
admit. The surrounding remedy surface is thinner. About 540 failure sites in
the scope packages pass an empty remedy. They fall back to the per-code
default, which for lifecycle.state is "run bootwright status ... to see the
records and the next step". status cannot show why a block failed, because an
effect attempt record cannot hold a failure (only an unknown resolution can).
It shows [FAIL] and the same Next the apply already printed. For a record that
cannot be decoded, the default sends the operator to status, which reads the
same record and refuses again. The default fills `<context>` only from the
`--context` flag. An invocation that uses the selected context, and 22
authored Ceph and substrate remedies, print the placeholder literally. Several
exits name no Bootwright command: "restore the target it ran against",
"restore X to what its frozen request names", "install bootwright X ... and
run controller install", "remove it with bootwright X", "destroy it with the
build that applied it". Two remedies can loop. An unattended destroy over an
incomplete apply is told to take the digest from `plan`, which previews the
apply continuation instead. A contradicted incomplete apply is told to review
status, which then offers no step at all. A destroy resolution defers to "this
result's last diagnostic", but the CLI re-sorts the diagnostics by code and
message before printing. Take-back destroy remedies omit the --authorize
tokens the spec requires.

Strengths to keep:

- contextCommand (commands.go:14) binds every engine-written remedy to the
  resolved context, so a copied lifecycle remedy never acts on another context.
- continuationCommand gives the exact continuation with every frozen token
  bound to its digest (authorizing), and uses the placeholder only for a removal
  whose plan is not yet fixed.
- status's offered() offers only commands whose decision would pass over the
  records it read, and refusalExit avoids offering a verb the records refuse.
- An operation record that cannot be decoded deliberately avoids pointing back
  at status and names the registering build (records.go:293-310), as the spec
  requires.
- An observation that could not run records its first diagnostic, bounded, on
  the resolution, so the refusal and a later status agree on the reason and
  remedy (observationFailure, unresolvedOf).

#### Lane O07

**Message quality of capability evidence refusals and their block framing**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Each capability's Go evidence check
is strict and fail-closed. It checks the request digest, the shape of the
frozen request and ownership, then each postcondition condition. An attempt
whose evidence fails these checks becomes unknown, never done. That is the
strong part. The thin part is what the operator learns. Almost all of the 259
refusal sentences are fixed text: about 12 name an object, about 207 carry no
remedy, and the code-wide default remedy ("run bootwright status ...") applies
to them. The messages fail at three layers. (1) Most Validate*Presence
functions first check the adapter's own `postcondition` flag. The Python
adapter computes that flag from almost the same conditions. So in every
observation of a drifted target, the decisive sentence is "\<adapter> did not
prove its postcondition", and the specific sentences behind it are reachable
only when Go and Python disagree. All 3 unresolved events in the owner's runs
read exactly that. (2) In a mutation, the adapter refuses to publish
incomplete evidence and fails with a named list of what is unmet. Go reports
only "the adapter operation did not complete", and the named list stays in the
root-owned raw output. (3) An attempt's own refusal diagnostic carries no
block or object. It is not written to the attempt record or the event log, so
status and logs cannot show it later. Status even says the attempt's outcome
"was not recorded". lifecycle.Drifted gives a good frame: the subject, the
host and the exact repeat command. But it throws away the capability's own
remedy and replaces it with "restore X to what its frozen request names", and
under destroy it can quote internal classification sentences as the cause. The
KubeVirt host proof (it carries Failures, names the provider and gives a
remedy) and the Ceph proofs (they name the object) show the pattern to
generalize. The evidence could safely carry object names: the frozen request
already holds every network, disk, unit and domain name, and the architecture
spec allows naming objects (but not values).

Strengths to keep:

- The evidence validation fails closed: a digest mismatch, a shape mismatch or
  an ownership doubt always leads to unknown, never done, and the read for a
  removal is kept separate from the apply's (Unremoved/Unfinished).
- The KubeVirt host proof (kubevirt/evidence.go:94-96) checks the adapter's
  named failures before the flag, names InfraProvider/\<name>, and gives a
  concrete input remedy. It is the model to generalize.
- lifecycle.Drifted/unresolvedFailure already frame a reason with the block
  id, a subject, the host (PlacedOn adds the address) and the exact command that
  observes again. The libvirt machine Unresolved names a foreign domain, an
  unanswering URI and a held socket specifically.
- Ceph proofs.go names the object in all 10 refusals, and some give an exact
  prerequisite command (apply CephSubvolume \<name> first).
- The Python unreached() already computes a safe, field-name-only unmet list
  for each capability, so the information Go needs exists and is secret-free.

#### Lane O08

**Real-run evidence A: the Ceph and single-node runs**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** In the real Ceph and single-node runs
the state machine held. No incident led to a wrong-target effect, a false done
or a lost block. Every unknown or canceled effect was observed before it was
retried. A partial or no-effect resolution was followed by a retry in the same
invocation, often within seconds. Interrupted operations (8 canceled attempts
in 2 operations) recovered on the next apply in under two minutes. Destroy
resolved unfinished apply blocks through the removal's own check (D119) even
when the apply's own observation failed. One apply operation was continued
across about 20 rebuilt executables over 10 hours and still converged. The
lab-5 and SNO runs were clean. The weak side is causes. Of 37 non-clean effect
attempts, none has its cause in any durable Bootwright record. The attempt log
records only the outcome word. The attempt state record may not carry a
failure at all; only an unknown resolution can. For Ceph, the retained adapter
output does not have the cause either: the role prints "the run names its
reason" and the reason goes only through a no_log protocol record. So the
remedy "inspect the retained operation evidence" sends the operator to files
that do not hold it. The cause survived only where a later resolution hit the
same refusal and logged observation-failed (12 events), and even then as
internal tokens and code sites. Outcome class comes from the diagnostic code,
not from what happened. Pre-effect Ceph boundary refusals (some ended 2
seconds in) are recorded unknown, which costs a resolution each time: 16 of 46
resolutions found no effect. A crash after a performed mutation is recorded
failed. operation.jsonl holds only "opened" lines: 16 invocations of one
operation and not one ending.

Strengths to keep:

- Unknown and canceled effects were never retried blind. Every one in the
  evidence (28 unknown, 8 canceled) was observed by a resolution before the next
  attempt, and a partial or no-effect resolution was followed by a retry in the
  same invocation, often within seconds.
- Interrupt recovery is clean: two interrupted operations each had 4 parallel
  attempts canceled, and the next apply resolved and converged them in under two
  minutes.
- Destroy over an incomplete apply worked even when the apply's own
  observation refused: the removal's own check (D119/D123) resolved the block
  no-effect, and the observation-failed and apply-observation events record why
  it fell back.
- Continuation across rebuilt executables worked: one operation converged
  across about 15 to 20 automation digests over 10 hours, with each attempt's
  build recorded (ranUnder).
- Resolution observation failures are durable and specific (ObservationFailure
  plus the observation-failed event with code and message). This is the model to
  extend to effect attempts.

#### Lane O09

**Real-run evidence B: the network-matrix, network-variants and cutoff runs**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Real runs in this lane: 10 unique
incident chains, with 19 failed, 33 canceled and 1 unknown attempt outcomes, 3
observation-failed and 3 unresolved events, and 40 resolutions. Incidents: -
**nv-cutoff (3 chains):** attempt 1 failed with the role's own clear refusal,
"declared network made \<ip> unreachable ... cannot change under this apply:
run bootwright destroy ...". The operator repeated apply, and attempt 2 re-ran
about 6 minutes of convergence and failed with the same text. Then came a
destroy, a corrected apply and a destroy. - **network-matrix op-797e60:** six
installs failed in the same second on a transient emulated-BMC HTTP 500. -
**op-d3b6ed:** the routing table was not under its owned unit. -
**op-b2d644:** a destroy failed because nmcli did not answer; a repeated
destroy recovered. - **op-d91bc0:** the substrate attempt came back unknown
even though the adapter exited 0 with completion evidence. A resolution 27
minutes later found it completed. A hosted-area mode refusal then failed
os-package-tree. - **op-5ec5ab and op-61985b:** two cancels, each resolved
partial, then a retry that succeeded. - **network-variants op-9323e0:** an
observation failed because a no_log protocol publish failed with a censored
cause. It stayed unknown until a resolution under a new build. -
**network-variants op-532b61:** a cancel during the installer wait became
unresolved, with a drift-style message. It resolved partial under a later
build. What works: cancel, resolution, retry is deterministic and recovered by
itself every time; repeated apply and destroy always found a way on. What is
thin: every role-level cause (19 of 19 failed attempts) reached Bootwright
only as the failed exit "the adapter operation did not complete". The attempt
event log and the attempt record keep no cause. The operation log holds only
"opened" records. Next always says `apply`, even when the role says only
destroy exits. So the operator learns why only by reading root-owned raw
Ansible output.

Strengths to keep:

- Cancel, resolution, retry is deterministic and recovered by itself in every
  real chain (op-5ec5ab, op-61985b, op-9323e0, op-532b61): six interrupted
  installs each resolved partial and the retry in the same invocation changed
  them, with idempotent fast-forward through boot and installation groups.
- The roles write excellent operator-facing causes, with object, address, what
  NetworkManager did, and the exact next command, for example network.yml's
  cut-off stop. The material for good diagnostics already exists; it only fails
  to reach the operator.
- Repeated destroy recovers a failed removal (op-b2d644 nmcli no-answer,
  replaced by op-81a5d4, done); a paused destroy waiting for Machines continued
  cleanly in op-fd93bc.
- The resolution record already carries ObservationFailure (code, bounded
  message, remedy), and `onlyExit` already marks a refusal whose only way on is
  destroy. Both are ready to generalize.
- Retained raw output was present and complete for every attempt, including
  the wedged and canceled ones, so the true cause of every incident in this lane
  was recoverable by a root reader.

#### Lane O10

**Operator documentation and runbooks for failure and recovery**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** For an operator, recovery is mostly
carried by the product's own output, not by the documentation. The strong
parts: every apply/destroy result ends with Logs, Follow and Next lines and a
stable receipt. Unknown blocks get a per-block Reason and Remedy in status
(lifecycle/unresolved.go). Interrupts exit 130 with the continuing command.
The guide states the last-resort deletion and what --allow-orphans abandons.
The thin parts: the most common failure class, an Ansible task failing inside
a role, reaches the operator as lifecycle.state "the adapter operation did not
complete". The role's precise message (which often holds the real remedy, e.g.
"run bootwright destroy ... correct ... then apply") lives only in the
root-owned raw output. The attempt record keeps no failure for a failed block.
status shows a reason only for unknown blocks. `logs` events show only
"outcome failed". One runbook concedes this in its own text and tells the
operator to read the file as root. The failed result's Next then says repeat
apply, which repeats the same failure. The operator guide has no
troubleshooting section. It has no vocabulary of operation or block states, no
exit-status table for effectful commands, and no list of or link to the
diagnostic codes. Its recovery rules (unknown versus failed, continue versus
destroy, the lost binding, build changes) sit under "Changing the build
between runs" and "Run a lab journey". The runbooks treat any unexpected
failure as "stop the run, clean up, start again" with no cleanup procedure.
They encode knowledge the product does not give (wait for an interrupted
installer guest to power off; do not stop guests merely because they are on).
Evidence preservation reads /var/log/bootwright directly with sudo find and
tar.

Strengths to keep:

- Unknown blocks carry a per-block Reason and Remedy that status prints and
  the refusal repeats (lifecycle/unresolved.go, output_status.go:392-400). The
  B1079 run shows these as 'Drifted' explanations naming the subject and host.
  This is the model to extend to failed blocks.
- Every apply/destroy result ends with Logs, Follow and an exact Next command
  with --context, plus a stable receipt whose next token maps to one command
  (specs/cli.md:825-899). An interrupted run writes its result before
  runtime.interrupted and exit 130.
- status offers only commands whose decisions would pass over the records it
  read, held by TestStatusStepsAreExactlyWhatTheVerbsDecisionsDerive
  (specs/cli.md:901-913), so it never suggests a command that refuses.
- The guide explains the interrupt model concretely: one or two Ctrl-C, sudo
  use_pty, tmux, and a systemd-run unit with its context named
  (operator-guide.md:709-731). It also states the last-resort deletion and what
  it abandons (906-917).
- The roles already compose operator-grade messages with object names and
  remedies (network.yml:252-262); the loss happens only at the Go boundary.

#### Lane O11

**plan and diff as the operator's prediction and diagnosis tools around a
failure**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Without --observe, diff reads records
only, under the shared lock. It never refuses a failed, paused or unknown
apply or destroy. It turns each unsettled object into an `unknown` row: "its
blocks read failed: \<ids>", "destroy \<op> has removed X and not yet Y", or
"the block record is lost". These rows name the block ids, and the remedy
points to `status`. Refusals come only from the lifecycle read: a lease, an
unreadable record, a retired index, or an input that does not compile. A
collected revision reads unknown and is not refused. That part is strong: no
failure leaves diff unusable. It is also honest: unknown never reads as
absent. With --observe, the code adds well-bounded refusals: a lost binding, a
context changed mid-read, an unbound host, a missing runtime. Each comes with
a specific remedy. The thin part is how an observation failure is explained.
The per-block reason drops the block id and usually the host. Only the first
unknown block's reason is kept. A capability's canned "returned no evidence"
text replaces the real error, and its remedy sends the operator to a
resolution log that diff never writes. Generic remedies say "restore what the
reason names" when the reason names nothing. A change of execution contract by
a build update refuses the whole observation, and the remedy is a destroy. The
plan preview of a continuation shows each block's state (failed, unknown,
running). Without --stage or --until it does not say which blocks the next
apply will resolve first and which it will retry, and it gives no cause. So
plan alone cannot tell a safe retry from an unproved outcome; only status can.
Plan shows authorizations, impacts, data-loss tokens, the Machines to stop and
another build's steps. It shows nothing about duration or likely failure.
Neither command tells drift from failure by itself: diff --observe shows
drift, status shows failure.

Strengths to keep:

- Plain diff never refuses because of a failed, paused, unknown or partly
  removed operation. Each such object becomes an unknown row naming its block
  ids, and unknown is never folded into absent (diff.go recordedSide,
  foldState).
- --observe refusals each carry a specific remedy that offers the safe
  fallback: the lost binding (diff_observe.go:60), the context that moved
  mid-read (:112) and the unbound host (via unobservedDiff).
- Observation is held to read-only by construction: Observe only, a read-only
  controller stage whose mutators refuse, produced material cleared unread, and
  a whole-comparison refusal when a projection carries lent Secret material.
- The plan preview takes the same decision path as the verb (preview,
  decideAs), so plan refuses exactly where apply or destroy would. It also shows
  the Requires tokens with digests, Stop first, Stop after online cleanup, Takes
  back and another build's steps.
- The diff Against, Input and Plan header lines separate 'records prove' from
  'read live', say when input changes will be refused or added, and point to
  status for the next step.

#### Lane X01

**Crash and kill walk through apply**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** A fresh apply writes, in order: (1)
claim \<op>/ with an empty blocks/; (2) set mutation.json to running; (3)
create a custody Secret binding; (4) in the registration transaction, write
the controller state.json binding, (5) the controller reservations, (6)
plan.json, (7) operation.json, (8) index.json, then mark log retention and
reclaim idle claims; (9) operation.jsonl "opened". For each block: (10)
state.json pending if absent, (11) attempt-N.json running, (12) state.json
running, (13) the attempt log, (14) the /run job directory with lent Secret
files and a scratch directory, (15) ansible-playbook and its remote effects,
(16) the preparation in the attempt record, (17) retained output, (18)
produced material in custody, (19) the attempt record set to observed, (20)
state.json with the outcome. Then (21) operation.json terminal, (22) the
mutation.json projection, (23) release of stale bindings. Every record write
is staged, fsynced, renamed, read back and directory-fsynced. A failure after
the rename is classed unknown. The next decision re-derives state from the
records, so no cut between two consecutive writes gave me a dead end. Each cut
leaves a condition that the next apply or destroy recognises and either
collects or re-observes: an idle claim, running evidence with no operation, an
unnamed binding, an adoptable start, a running block, a lagging operation
record or projection. SIGKILL of the elevated child ends the local adapter
tree through the parent-death signal. A later run sweeps the stale job. The
weak side is what the operator is told. None of the 1,935 real attempt logs
records a cause. operation.jsonl records only "opened". A run deadline is
reported as a plain unresolved outcome. A log-area ENOSPC loses its errno. Two
cuts are handled by re-observation although the spec says nothing was
recorded: a proved attempt record beside a lagging block record, and the
in-memory unknown written after a completion failed to publish. Remote effects
continue after a local kill. Only the capability's observation stands between
that and a retry.

Strengths to keep:

- Every record publication is staged, fsynced, read back, renamed with a
  replace guard, read back again and directory-fsynced
  (internal/workspace/contextfs/publication_linux_amd64.go:47-96). A failure
  after the rename is classified unknown rather than failed, so no cut leaves a
  torn record.
- Outcomes and releases are written under recordingContext
  (context.WithoutCancel, attempts.go:27), and the scheduler waits for in-flight
  blocks instead of abandoning them (scheduler.go:161-172). Cancellation never
  suppresses the record of an attempt that already ran.
- Registration has an explicit three-valued outcome (notRegistered,
  registered, possiblyRegistered; registration.go:18-30) that decides exactly
  what to give back, so evidence and bindings are never released for an
  operation that may own them.
- StartAttempt writes the block record before the exclusive attempt record,
  then the counting block record, and adopts only a provably effect-free
  interrupted start (store.go:974-1073). Attempt numbers stay monotonic across
  crashes.
- The local process tree dies with its invocation: GuardParent's PDEATHSIG on
  the elevated child, the adapter's parent-death signal, and lock-based sweeps
  of stale jobs. Kernel flocks for the lease mean a crash never leaves a stale
  context lock.

#### Lane X02

**Crash and kill walk through destroy**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Destroy is a sequence of
independently atomic file publications under the context lease. There is no
all-or-nothing transaction: `MutateLifecycle` says "Every publication this
transaction performs is independently atomic". In order, a fresh destroy over
an apply: (1) lists bindings; (2) decides under the shared lock and may
finalize first; (3) optionally binds a rebind; (4) under the lease, re-proves
the basis. Over an incomplete apply it records the apply's state from its
blocks and projects it. Each unproved block then gets StartResolution, a
read-only observation, a custody capture, CompleteResolution and the apply
record again. (5) Probes quiescence (reads, plus KubeVirt lends). (6) Raises
destroy-running evidence, then writes plan.json, operation.json and the index.
(7) Per block: marks the reservation releasing, StartAttempt, the
keep-before-removal custody publication, the inverse, CompleteAttempt. (8)
finish: operation done, withdraw custody, release reservations. (9) Outside
the lease: release each binding, then a second lease publishes pristine
evidence and reclaims. (10) Collects stranded bindings. Every SIGKILL between
two of these writes is re-decided from durable state. The next destroy
finalizes, continues, resolves or replaces. The next apply finalizes a
completed removal or refuses an incomplete one. The kill harness drives every
write point with an empty kill ledger. Custody is withdrawn only after the
record reads done, so no cut loses the only copy of produced material.
Reservations and bindings that outlive a cut are released by the next verb or
by context deletion. The thin parts are what the operator is told and a few
corners. A completed removal whose withdrawal or reservation release fails
prints an empty receipt and a raw store error. An unprovable effect on a dead
host leads only to deletion, yet the remedy loops on 'repeat destroy'. A build
update can make the registering build the only exit. A registration cut after
plan.json lands leaks a directory nothing reclaims or reports. A destroy
paused at the stop boundary prints OK yet exits with an error.

Strengths to keep:

- An exhaustive kill harness
  (internal/reconciliation/lifecycle/kill_harness_test.go) kills each journey at
  every durable write and holds convergence to a one-invocation bound, with an
  empty kill ledger. The observable end state (evidence, reservations, bindings,
  custody, idle claims) is compared too.
- Post-completion work runs under recordingContext (context.WithoutCancel),
  and every release is idempotent (keyring Release and Withdraw return false
  when nothing is held). finalized() reads durable evidence, so a removal whose
  record reads done is always finished by the next destroy or apply.
- Custody ordering prevents losing the only copy of produced material.
  Material is withdrawn only once the removal record reads done. A failed
  publication records unknown, never failed. The work-area copy is published
  unproved before the inverse that deletes it, so a cut leaves it in custody, in
  the work area, or both.
- Every transition re-proves its basis under the exclusive lock. A removal is
  planned only from the frozen plan and resolves every unproved block before it
  registers, so a refusal before registration leaves the context as found apart
  from the resolutions it proved.
- Context deletion is intent-journaled (Deleting mode, then directory removal,
  then claims and logs, then the registry). Its non-pristine refusal names the
  destroy that finishes a lagging removal.

#### Lane X03

**Dead-end census: every state whose exit is deletion, backup, another build
or nothing**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Terminal states are designed with
care. A completed destroy holding a block that is not done, records no index
accounts for, a lost frozen Secret binding, unreadable mutation evidence and a
lost context directory each have a dedicated refusal. These refusals name the
exit the context guard admits, and they compute the exact `--allow-orphans`
form from the guard's own reading of the evidence (deletionCommand).
Transitions refuse before any effect, registration or release, so reaching a
dead end never makes things worse. The weak point is how often the only exit
is outside Bootwright. Four classes stand out: 1. **Build update.** A fresh
removal proves every owned block's execution-contract fingerprint and content
digest against the running build (freshDestroy calls proveContracts, which
calls executionContracts). This also applies to a completed apply. Contract
goldens move in about one commit in eleven, so after an ordinary build update
a provisioned environment can often be removed only by the registering build.
Bootwright does not retain that build, and the "take stock" step in the
operator guide lists only unfinished operations. 2. **A target that cannot be
observed.** If a block's host died or its object was destroyed by hand, the
removal registers nothing. The only exits are to "restore the target" or to
abandon the whole context. 3. **Remedies naming exits that do not exist.** A
remedy may name a matching backup, which the spec says is not a supported
exit. It may name a registering build whose identity cannot be reproduced (a
modified build) or is the running build. Or it may send the operator to
`status`, which then offers no step. 4. **Bounds that never retire** (retained
operations, keyring identities, tool sources), whose exit is deletion and
re-init. The flow is thin on narrower exits: per-block abandonment, retention
of the registering executable, a compatibility forecast before a build switch,
and pruning.

Strengths to keep:

- Terminal-state refusals compute the exact deletion the guard will admit from
  the guard's own reading of the evidence (deletionCommand), so
  `--allow-orphans` appears exactly when needed and the 'cannot list' caveat
  appears over unreadable evidence.
- Every dead end refuses before any effect, registration, binding or release
  (proveShared runs under the shared lock before presentation), so reaching one
  never deepens the damage.
- The lost-binding refusal lists every object the operation owns, because
  nothing can list them after the deletion. Other abandonment paths should copy
  this.
- canTakeBack proves the removal would actually plan (contracts plus
  removalOf) before status or a remedy offers it, which avoids most remedy loops
  for another-build continuations.
- Host-identity change has a real, narrow Bootwright exit (`controller
  rebind`) instead of a deletion.

#### Lane X04

**Unprovable outcomes: blocks that can stay unknown because the target is gone
or silent**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The lane's guarantee is strong and
uniform: an observation that fails, is silent, foreign, malformed or
contradictory is recorded `unknown`, never `no-effect` (observedEffect,
ReadEffect, removalEffect), and an unknown block admits nothing. A fresh
destroy over an incomplete apply first reads the apply's Observe, and if that
does not prove completion it falls back to the removal's own check (D119).
Several capabilities have a removal check that is local or synthesized:
hardware, baremetal, add-on and networking retirement, agent-install
controller side, and Ceph retired with Bootwright-owned virtual hosts. For
those, a dead cluster API or a lost Ceph quorum still resolves by itself. A
foreign or drifted target is explained by the capability's Unresolved reporter
and resolves once the operator restores the target. Where the thin spots are:
the target is permanently silent (a dead remote hypervisor and its emulated
BMC, a dead KubeVirt host cluster, a dead SSH provider host). Then (a) the
quiescence gate reads silence as `lifecycle.live` and names `bootwright
machine stop`, which needs the same silent controller, so the remedy loops;
(b) an unknown block's resolution refusal and status say "restore the target"
and "repeat destroy" forever; (c) a done block whose inverse must reach the
dead host fails every destroy, and the replacing destroy retries the same
inverse. In all three cases destroy can never finish. The only exit, `context
delete --purge --allow-orphans`, is policy (D38, Q92 answered by D183), but
none of these refusals names it. Observation failures from an unreachable host
surface as "the adapter operation did not complete", which names no host. The
one precedent of a scoped operator acknowledgement that a target is gone is
`--unregistered`, plus the erase relaxation.

Strengths to keep:

- Unknown never reads as no-effect: observedEffect forces unknown on any run
  error or out-of-vocabulary effect, and removalEffect maps only completed,
  no-effect and partial, so a silent or foreign target can never be counted as
  removed (attempts.go:366-393).
- The D119 fallback lets a fresh destroy resolve an apply block through the
  removal's own check. Capabilities with local or synthesized removal checks
  (hardware, baremetal, add-ons, networking, agent-install controller side, Ceph
  retired with virtual hosts) therefore resolve even when the cluster API or
  Ceph quorum is gone.
- Every unresolved block carries a reason and remedy read from the same
  durable resolution record, so the destroy refusal and a later status agree
  (unresolved.go:126-155).
- libvirt quiescence takes the emulated BMC's power state as a second opinion
  when the hypervisor is silent, so a lone dead libvirtd does not block removal
  when the BMC answers (capability.go:551-559).
- Scoped operator acknowledgements already exist and are the model to
  generalize: --unregistered for an unreadable guest registration and
  --authorize erase=\<m>:retain for an erase the operator waives.

#### Lane X05

**Concurrency: two invocations, stale locks, shared hosts and concurrent
commands**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Concurrency rests on three kernel
flocks and on durable claims. The host-wide root lock (shared for reads,
exclusive for publication, a 1-minute wait for mutators, no wait for readers)
and the per-context lease (exclusive for lifecycle effects, shared for bounded
runs, never waits) are flocks on directories opened close-on-exec, so a killed
holder never leaves them held. Adapter jobs in /run add a job lock that the
supervisor, ansible-playbook and workers inherit and a holder lock only the
invocation holds. Parent-death signals and a killpg end the tree, and a sweep
reaps free jobs on the next run. Host reservations in the controller record
are durable and release only through destroy, the next apply or an orphaning
delete. Their conflict diagnostics name the holding context, key and object,
and they say which destroy to run. Registration copes with in-flight
concurrent applies through directory claims, re-proof and evidence
restoration. This is careful and mostly strong. It is thin in what it tells
the operator. A lease or root refusal says only "context state is held by
another mutator" or "context storage is busy", with "retry after the running
Bootwright command finishes". It does not say which command holds it, which
operation, whether a lifecycle or a short read, or for how long. Status probes
no lease, so it cannot tell a live apply from an interrupted one. Readers do
not retry. Bounded reads such as `machine list --power-status` are refused for
an apply's whole lifetime with the same text. There are also a few
unenumerated pairs. Two contexts that each use the other's managed bridge make
both destroys refuse, each naming the other. A power run checks other
contexts' BMC holds only at admission and holds no claim. A restoration after
a lease refusal is refused for the same reason. A failed sweep of any
context's stale job stops every context's adapters without naming the
directory.

Strengths to keep:

- Every lock is a kernel flock on a close-on-exec descriptor
  (nativefs/open_linux.go), so a killed holder never leaves the root lock or a
  lease held, and no lock is ever taken over.
- The adapter job design (jobs_linux_amd64.go) separates the inherited job
  lock from the invocation-only holder lock. Its refusal therefore names
  context, block, operation and Machine for a live holder, and the lock path for
  orphaned descendants. With a parent-death signal plus killpg in the
  supervisor, and ControlPath=none in ansible.cfg, this leaves no surviving SSH
  masters.
- Host reservation conflict diagnostics (hostreservation.go) name the holding
  context, the key (or only its class when it could be private), both objects by
  API kind, and a remedy naming the holder's destroy or the field that chooses
  the key. The releasing mark is durable across interruption.
- Registration's claim/raise/re-proof protocol (registration.go) handles
  concurrent in-flight applies, restores evidence only when provably its own,
  and never collects what a newer invocation raised.
- logs --follow already probes the lease without blocking and retries busy
  polls, which is a ready mechanism to extend to status and decisions.

#### Lane X06

**Build and version skew between a failed operation and its recovery**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** When a new build meets an operation
an older build registered, the lane checks several things in order: record
decoding (closed, canonical, one version), the runtime closure (lock digest
plus Python ABI), and since a01f9a1db on 2026-11-15 a per-implementation
execution-contract fingerprint for every saved block. Every check refuses
before any effect and before any record moves. That part is strong: nothing is
half-continued, the automation digest alone never refuses, and a pure
automation fix continues. It is thin in what it leaves the operator. The
fingerprint is a SHA-256 of the whole contract golden text. That text includes
package-qualified Go type names and every nested request and evidence field. A
fix that touches a capability's Go types, even a package rename, moves the
fingerprint. Twenty of the 401 commits since 2026-11-15 moved at least one
fingerprint, and os-install-anaconda-v1 and physical-erase-v1 moved six times
each. A moved contract refuses three things: continuation, the fresh destroy
under the new build of every started block (canTakeBack and freshDestroy both
prove contracts), and even the destroy of a completed apply. The only exit is
"install bootwright devel (\<commit>)". Nothing keeps that binary: `make build`
overwrites bin/bootwright, there are no tags, and a dirty build's identity is
recorded without its modified flag. When the defect sits in the observation or
removal path, the old build cannot finish the destroy either, and the operator
is left with `context delete --purge --allow-orphans`. scripts/check-commits
under-reports these breaks. The operator guide still describes the replaced
re-planning rule.

Strengths to keep:

- Every build-skew check (record decode, closure, contracts, frozen-request
  read, removal re-derivation) runs under the shared lock before presentation
  and again before registration, and refuses before any restore, bind,
  observation or write. A refused build never leaves a half-continued operation.
- The automation digest alone never refuses: automation-only and pin-free
  fixes continue, and each attempt records the build that ran it
  (Attempt.Build), which is good raw material for naming the right recovery
  build.
- canTakeBack narrows the take-back offer to started blocks, so a contract
  move confined to unstarted work still lets the current build supersede the
  operation (pinned by tests).
- Decode refusals extract only a uniquely and exactly spelled `executable` or
  `build` member to name the registering build, and handle the 'this executable'
  self-reference for attempt records.
- The contract guard (TestEveryImplementationContractMatchesItsGolden plus the
  manifest check) makes the shipped manifest reproducible from code, and make
  build refuses to produce a binary with a stale manifest.

#### Lane X07

**External dependency failures: network, DNS, proxy, time, credentials,
certificates and disk space**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Faults outside Bootwright's control,
like an unreachable host, a failed DNS lookup, a proxy refusal, a TLS failure,
a wrong credential, clock skew or a full disk, are handled fail-closed and
with safe retries. They are not explained to the operator. Retries are
careful: SSH never reconnects (ServerAliveInterval 15 x 3, no ansible
reconnection_retries). Redfish resends a write only when the request provably
never left. KubeVirt retries only idempotent requests on 429/502/503/504 or a
refused connection. Ceph package downloads retry three times on
transport_faults.lost and truncate the partial file before each retry. The
context store maps ENOSPC/EDQUOT/EFBIG to a free-space remedy. Only one
adapter turns these faults into classes with the endpoint named: the
controller stage (dns, certificate, timeout, unreachable, proxy, status,
redirect, integrity, trust, storage). Go reads that vocabulary only in
internal/controller/ansiblelocal (prerequisites.AdapterRefusal), and Python
classifies with it only in controller_files.py. Every lifecycle adapter
instead builds its own closed reason map (Invocation.Refusals), and many build
none: the libvirt host and machine, the KubeVirt host, hardware, disk
discovery, the host firewall, and managed services past readiness. An SSH
target that cannot be reached, a host-key mismatch, a full /tmp, or a failed
task under no_log all end as FailedExit: lifecycle.state "the adapter
operation did not complete", naming no host, no class and no cause. Its remedy
points at a raw output file only root can read. Where a reason map exists, it
often folds several classes together. Redfish calls a 401 "did not answer".
Mirror fill puts DNS, credential and disk-full under "image-unreachable".
Hosted RHSM sends TLS failures to "check the organization and activation key".
The Go messages also drop the errno of a full log root or a full staging area.
Whether a fault leaves its block failed or unknown depends on which diagnostic
code the message's author chose (AttemptOutcome), not on a table. An adapter
run that reaches its deadline ends with no diagnostic at all.

Strengths to keep:

- The controller stage's closed acquisition classes
  (prerequisites.adapterConditions) name the source host, or the tool area for
  storage, give a specific correction for each class, distinguish failed from
  unknown by whether the acknowledgement was delivered, and let no adapter text
  through. This is the model to generalize.
- Retries respect effect safety: SSH never reconnects (security.md, B1045),
  Redfish resends a write only when it provably never left (unsent) or is
  repeatable, KubeVirt retries only idempotent requests, and Ceph package
  downloads truncate partial bytes before each retry. transport_faults.lost
  keeps certificate, HTTP-status and NXDOMAIN failures out of the retry path.
- The context store turns ENOSPC/EDQUOT/EFBIG into 'the filesystem holding the
  state root has no room: ... (ENOSPC)' with a free-space remedy and never
  treats a capacity error as damage (contextfs ioDiagnosis).
- The KubeVirt provider proof surfaces its first failed check with the check's
  name, and on 401/403 names the exact exit, '--authorize rebind=\<kubeconfig
  Secret>'. The managed-OS registration and Ceph tiebreaker refusals likewise
  name the Machine, the endpoint and a working exit (including destroy
  --unregistered).
- Go's media and acquisition fetchers (medialocal, internal/acquisition)
  separate DNS (including resolver timeout), untrusted certificate (unknown
  authority, hostname, expired or not yet valid), timeout and unreachable, and
  name the host. Each message points to a different operator action.

#### Lane X08

**Timeouts, waits, hangs and cancellation**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The process side of waits and
cancellation is strong. Every lifecycle adapter run has a deadline (the
request's own, derived from frozen budgets, else 2 hours). A deadline or a
cancel follows one path: SIGTERM to the Python supervisor, which is a child
subreaper and kills every descendant within TERMINATION_BOUND (5 s). The Go
side then kills the process group once the adapter is reaped or the 5 s drain
passes. Pdeathsig is armed on a locked OS thread, so a Bootwright that dies
takes its adapters with it. The first Ctrl-C prints the operation result, the
log location and the next command, and exits 130. Root lock waits are bounded
at 1 minute and can be cancelled. The thin parts are reporting and naming. (1)
When a run hits its own deadline, the runner returns a bare
context.DeadlineExceeded. The scheduler treats that as an operator
cancellation and drops it, so the operator gets only "an effect has an
unresolved outcome". The attempt log records only "unknown", and nothing says
a deadline of N hours passed for block X. (2) A second Ctrl-C ends the process
with no message, leaving attempts `running`. (3) The roles write good expiry
messages (budget, Machine, last answer, a resume hint for the agent install).
They reach only the retained adapter output; stderr shows "the adapter
operation did not complete". (4) During a long wait, liveness is only "still
running, \<elapsed>". No row shows the bound, and some long Ceph blocks emit no
group rows. (5) Remote commands started over SSH can keep running after
cancel, despite the runner comment "No adapter effect outlives cancellation"
(tracked as B573 for Ceph).

Strengths to keep:

- The adapter tree termination is carefully layered. Pdeathsig is armed on a
  goroutine locked to its OS thread. The Python supervisor is a child subreaper
  that kills every descendant, including workers in their own sessions, within
  TERMINATION_BOUND before its own group kill. Go then kills the group after
  reap or drain. Every step is bounded (5 s plus 5 s).
- Run deadlines are derived from the frozen request's own budgets, plus
  margins, and honored unclamped. The documented bounds table is held to the
  code by TestDocumentedBoundsMatchCode, and families that hold to MaxDeadline
  refuse a request past it at planning, naming the object (e.g. ceph
  materials.go:236).
- The first interrupt is handled well. No new block is admitted, in-flight
