  attempts are awaited and recorded canceled, and the CLI prints the block
  table, the log location and the exact next command before runtime.interrupted
  with exit 130.
- Role waits follow the ansible-core lessons. Guarded until expressions,
  failed_when false with a separate assert outside no_log, and per-attempt
  bounds computed inside each attempt. Many fail_msg texts name the Machine, the
  budget and the last answer.
- containercluster_install_wait classifies installer outcomes (budget-spent,
  timeout, stalled, host-error) and gives each a precise hint. This is a ready
  model for a typed wait-expiry vocabulary.

#### Lane X09

**Destroy data safety: ownership proofs, wrong-target risk and authorization**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Destroy's data-safety gates are
front-loaded and read-only: under the exclusive lock a fresh removal re-proves
the controller host, re-proves its basis operation, resolves every unproved
block of the replaced lineage (proveRemovable), then probes quiescence of
every block (proveQuiescent), and only then registers. Any refusal leaves the
context as found, except that the replaced operation's record is deliberately
rewritten to the state its resolved blocks give. Authorization is tight:
tokens the plan does not consume refuse, unattended runs must bind data-loss
to a digest over each consuming step's identity, content and request digests
plus any erase relaxation, and a removal continuation only accepts its frozen
relaxation set. Context deletion re-decides under the transaction and refuses
when it differs from what was confirmed. Where it is thin: ownership is proved
by name in the libvirt, hosted-area, unit and package-tree paths (B568), so an
object an abandoned same-name context left reads as owned. The libvirt Machine
removal treats an absent domain as license to delete the name-derived disk
directory, controller unit and container. A provider-host removal still stops
owned managed networks without asking which guests use them (B567; trunks are
now guarded). Retained physical Machines and the services they use always read
quiescent (B571). On output, the quiescence probe throws away the cause of an
unreadable power state and offers a stop command that cannot work when the
hypervisor is down. The orphan-acknowledged delete under --yes never shows its
same-name hazard or its inventory, and the result names neither. Ownership
refusals in the roles reach the operator only as Ansible fail_msg text, not as
Go diagnostics with a code.

Strengths to keep:

- KubeVirt ownership is not name-derived: the owner annotation hashes the
  random operation id, block, kind, namespace and name, a creation after
  registration is required, and UID receipts take precedence
  (ansible/.../module_utils/kubevirt_machine.py:54-89). It is the model B568
  should generalize.
- Physical erase custody lives beneath the immutable apply operation id, and a
  fresh removal never adopts another removal's custody or receipt; it sets them
  aside as superseded and keeps only a bounded number.
- The data-loss digest binds each consuming step's ID, kind, object,
  implementation, content digest and request digest plus the relaxation.
  Inapplicable tokens refuse, and unattended runs must bind the digest. Every
  refusal prints the exact passing command (authorization.go:28-80).
- Resolution and quiescence run read-only under the exclusive lock before
  registration, and every block is probed, so one refusal lists everything to
  stop.
- Context deletion re-decides under its transaction, including an evidence and
  index digest, and refuses if the result differs from what was confirmed
  (service.go:683).

#### Lane X10

**Sensitive material in failure paths, and causes hidden by censoring**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** On the secrecy side the slice holds
up well. Lent material lives only in the job under /run (tmpfs) at 0600. The
runner refuses a material value that contains a lent part. Variables go
through a file and never through argv. The censored callback drops the
exception, warnings and deprecations of a censored result. Private log records
are normalized, bounded and stripped of control bytes. Across 29 real runs I
found no credential pattern in any retained output or attempt log. There are
two thin spots on the secrecy side. The private-publication token, the one
secret that protects the recovery passphrase and the registration material,
goes into the argv of mv/chcon. A credential-bearing media URL is also written
into the adapter scratch, which sits on persistent /var/lib and survives a
crash until the next run's sweep. The opposite risk is where this slice is
weakest. 563 of 651 no_log tasks can fail. When one fails, the operator gets
only its task name and ansible-core's censored notice. Go collapses that to
`lifecycle.state` "the adapter operation did not complete", and the remedy
points at the retained output, which holds nothing more. The worst case is the
completion phase (77 sites). Its message `unreached(...)` was written to name
field names only, so it would be safe to print, but the task-level no_log
censors it. This is visible in real runs: one Ceph apply and three managed-OS
resolutions failed with no cause anywhere. The same holds for six authored
fail_msg asserts that check a public marker, among them the wrong-disk
refusal, and for the fixed fail_json messages of no_log effect modules such as
the physical erase. The log-fault latch is sound, but it throws away the
area's own cause. The retained output keeps the head of a run and loses the
tail when it is cut.

Strengths to keep:

- Lent material is confined to a /run (tmpfs) job at 0600. Variables reach
  ansible-playbook only through a file, and checkMaterials refuses a material
  value that contains any lent part (process_linux_amd64.go:197-204). None of
  the 29 real runs' retained outputs or attempt logs shows a credential pattern.
- The censored callback is small and correct against ansible-core 2.21.5
  PRESERVE: it drops exception, warnings and deprecations for a censored result,
  covers loop items through _ansible_no_log, and is proved end to end by
  test_censored_output.py.
- Private log records are normalized (safeLogText strips control bytes and
  bounds every field), truncation is explicit, and group events reserve a 32 KiB
  tail so outcome lines always land.
- The log boundary is a real latch: the first failure cancels in-flight work,
  is recorded outside cancellation, and is cleared only by a later invocation
  that proves the boundary again.
- The 'register under no_log, then refuse outside no_log with the controller's
  printable, bounded line' pattern (boot.yml:66-85, physical_erase refused.yml)
  shows the right shape, including token redaction before printing.

#### Lane X11

**Partial runs: stage selection, pauses, independent branches and what the
result says**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The scheduler is careful about state.
It drains every block in flight, even when cancelled, before it stops. It
re-reads a block record whenever a start or resolution fails to publish. It
joins causes in frozen plan order, so which block finishes first never changes
what gets recorded. It decides "paused" with one explicit predicate: no
cancel, no log fault, no unstarted attempt, pending work left and nothing
unproved. Stage refusals happen before registration and name the exact `apply
--stage ...` that would unblock the work. Operation state comes from one
precedence function, NextOperationState. The weak part is what the operator
sees. The result is a list of rows (DONE, FAIL, PENDING, RUNNING, UNKNOWN),
and BlockResult has no field for why a block is pending. Four different
situations print as the same `[PENDING] ... (pending)` row: a block waiting on
a failed dependency, an independent block held back by the "no new first
attempt after a worked failure" rule, a block outside `--stage`/`--until`, and
a block never reached because of a cancel or a log fault. The code already
computes deferral reasons (reconciliation.Deferrals, planPreview), but only
for a preview with a selection. Failure diagnostics are forwarded without
their block's identity, while warnings get the block's object attached. When
parallel branches both fail, the operator cannot match causes to [FAIL] rows.
A paused result does not say what paused it. A paused destroy prints a green
"Destroy paused" headline but exits 1. An invocation that stopped without
failing reads "! Apply running" and offers `logs --follow`. A continuation
preview with no selection does not mark what will be retried or started, so
repeating the command does not say what it will do.

Strengths to keep:

- The scheduler drains every in-flight block before it returns, even on cancel
  or a log fault, so no attempt is abandoned and no outcome is lost
  (scheduler.go:161-173).
- Causes are joined in frozen plan order and warnings are sorted by position,
  so concurrent completion order never changes what is reported or recorded
  (scheduler.go:435-449, 105).
- Pause is decided by one explicit predicate (no cancel, no log fault, no
  unstarted attempt, nothing unproved, pending remains), and operation state by
  one precedence function (NextOperationState).
- Stage and --until refusals happen before registration and name the exact
  widened apply with every authorization token (decision.go:396-440). The
  preview derives from the same firstAdmission function the scheduler uses.
- An interrupted lifecycle keeps its result rows, Next command and receipt,
  and exits 130 with runtime.interrupted (cli/results.go:71-85).

#### Lane X13

**Test coverage of failure and recovery journeys**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Failure and recovery testing here is
unusually strong at one layer and thin at the edges. The kill harness
(TestAJourneyKilledAtAnyWriteLeavesAUsableStoreAndConvergesOnRetry) replays 14
lifecycle journeys and kills each one at every durable write, including the
custody and Secret-binding publications. For each kill it checks that the
records read back, that status and plan do not error, that no block runs under
pristine evidence, that no effect goes unrecorded, and that one retry
converges. Its ledger is exact and empty today. TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec
holds all five spec tables to the code. Precedence is enumerated over every
sequence of up to three blocks. The state-machine rows are driven through real
harness arrangements, and the status-parity tests run the verbs status offers,
so remedy loops are caught. The memoryArea double injects failure before a
write lands, after it lands, and when bounds or entries run out. The thin
parts: (1) the harness runs at Concurrency 1, while production runs 8 blocks
at once; (2) it models a crash as a failed write and never a cancellation; (3)
it skips the paused, live-quiescence, typed removal failure, additive, lineage
and relaxation journeys; (4) it never checks what the operator is told after a
kill; (5) classify, the single transition rule, is tested with 36 hand-picked
rows, not the whole input space; (6) the lifecycle judge's mapping from
adapter endings to codes is the one place that decides failed (retry) versus
unknown, and six of its endings have no test; (7) no fitness check requires a
block's failure to name its block or carry a remedy of its own; (8) the CLI
failure goldens render diagnostics written by hand, not what the engine
composes. So the machine's decisions are well pinned. Whether it tells the
operator anything useful is barely tested.

Strengths to keep:

- The kill harness kills 14 lifecycle journeys at every durable write,
  including custody and Secret-binding publications. Each kill must leave
  readable records and the invariants (nothing realized or past pending under
  pristine evidence, no unrecorded effect) and converge in one retry. Its exact,
  shrinking ledger is empty today. This is the base a state-machine conformance
  suite should build on.
- TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec parses all five spec tables, drives the real
  code with every row and covers each declared vocabulary. Operation precedence
  is enumerated over every block sequence of up to three, at and away from a
  pause boundary.
- The status-parity tests (decideCandidate) run each step status offers and
  require it to decide or name the same exits, which guards against remedy loops
  for the arranged states.
- The memoryArea double injects failure before a write lands, after it lands,
  and when byte or entry bounds run out, and a landing hook can stop an
  invocation exactly at a durable write.
- The ansiblerunner tests drive real child processes that break the protocol,
  hold descendants, ignore SIGTERM and keep output, and assert the tree is
  reaped and the outcome stays unknown.

#### Lane X14

**State machine extraction: the apply side**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The apply side is a five-level
machine: context, operation, block, attempt or resolution, adapter run. Only
its middle levels are tabled. classify() (transitions.go:41) is a real, pure
transition function over (requested verb, standing) with 8 outcomes.
AttemptTransition, ResolutionTransition and NextOperationState are pure too,
and TestTransitionTablesMatchSpec holds them to four spec tables. That core is
strong: every outcome outside the vocabulary folds to unknown, cancellation is
recorded under WithoutCancel, an unstarted attempt is told apart from a
started one, and a crash leaves a durable `running` block that the next verb
resolves first. The thin part is everything around classify. About 14 further
decisions are made by ad-hoc early returns in decideFrom/decideBy before or
after the switch: unindexed records, unclaimed evidence, finalization due,
erase relaxation, lost block records, contradictions, stage and --until
selection, changed input, additive refusal and others. Finalization is decided
three times. The removal's-check table and the inconclusive guard sit outside
the tested functions. The operation record has five writers. The terminal
write derives the operation state from the scheduler's in-memory block map,
not from the durable records the precedence table names. On failure output,
the one state that carries the most operator-relevant information, a `failed`
block, persists no cause at all. The attempt record has no failure member, and
the attempt log records only `outcome: failed`. So once the terminal output is
gone, the machine knows that a block failed but never why.

Strengths to keep:

- classify() is a single pure transition rule over (requested verb, standing),
  and the same function feeds both the decision and status's nextAction. That
  gives the explicit machine a real core to grow from.
- AttemptTransition, ResolutionTransition and NextOperationState are pure.
  Their spec tables are enforced exhaustively, including every block-state
  sequence up to length 3 at and away from a boundary.
- Outcomes are recorded under recordingContext (WithoutCancel), so an
  interruption never loses a proved outcome. Anything outside the vocabulary
  folds to unknown.
- Unstarted is distinguished from started (an empty state plus a durable
  re-read), so an attempt that never ran is never recorded as an effect.
- The unresolved-outcome diagnostic (unresolved.go:116) is the model stop: it
  names the block, persists the cause in the resolution's bounded failure
  member, and gives the exact command that observes it again.

#### Lane X15

**State machine extraction: the destroy side**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The destroy machine sits in three
places. classify() in transitions.go is a pure function of (requested verb,
held verb, held state, whether any block is not done, whether any block is
unknown, additive) and returns eight transition kinds. decideBy() adds guards
the table does not show: the erase-relaxation supersede, the contradiction
refusals, the lost-binding refusal and the continuation proofs. The
exclusive-lock run (executor.run) adds the rest of the destroy-only flow, in
order: host proof, then resolution of the superseded apply's unproved blocks
(written durably into the apply's records before the removal registers), then
the survivor and quiescence gates, then registration (raise evidence, publish
the index), then the scheduler with its pre-stop and online boundaries, then
finish. Finalization of a removal is a chain of separate durable steps, and
each can fail: record done, withdraw custody and release reservations (one
transaction), release each binding (outside any transaction), then publish
pristine evidence (a second transaction). The context deletion guard is the
outermost level and reads only one bit: whether the evidence is pristine.
Strengths: every decision is re-proved under the exclusive lock, no unproved
effect ever admits a removal, and an interrupted registration or finalization
is always recovered by repeating the verb. Weaknesses: a running, paused or
unknown removal has no superseding exit when the build changes. A failure
after the removal record reads done reaches the operator as a raw store error.
Pause causes, phase membership and pre-registration resolutions are not
durable states of their own. Several remedies name an older build, a store
restore or an orphaning deletion.

Strengths to keep:

- Before it resolves, gates or registers, every destroy transition re-proves
  under the exclusive lock the exact basis it was decided from: operation,
  record, plan digest, block states and attempt counts
  (proveRemovable→verifyBasis, finalize, completeRemoval, releaseUnclaimed).
- No unproved effect ever admits a removal. Resolutions run first, and when
  they cannot prove an effect the removal refuses with 'registered nothing'. The
  apply observation is tried before the removal check, so produced material is
  captured before any inverse runs.
- The registration outcome is a three-valued variable (notRegistered,
  registered, possiblyRegistered) that decides exactly what to give back. It is
  a model for making the other steps' implicit states explicit.
- Once the record reads done, finalization runs under recordingContext
  (cancellation cannot stop it), and evidence that is not pristine marks the
  bookkeeping still owed, so any later verb completes it.
- The quiescence gate probes every block and lists every stop command at once,
  both before registration and at the boundaries. The spec state table is tested
  by driving real journeys for each row (transitions_spec_test.go).

#### Lane X16

**Operator journeys through a failing apply, end to end**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** When a block fails, the apply keeps
durable truth well. Each attempt records `running` before its effect.
Cancellation waits for the blocks in flight. A canceled or unproved attempt
becomes `unknown`, and the next run resolves it from live evidence instead of
guessing. The stop always leaves the operator a result, a log location, a
`Next` command and a receipt, and an interrupt exits 130 naming the
continuation. Changed-input refusals, adapter-lock contention and state-root
capacity failures say what happened and name both ways out. The output is weak
at the moment that matters most: the cause of a failed block. A non-zero
`ansible-playbook` exit becomes one constant sentence, "the adapter operation
did not complete", plus a pointer to a root-owned file. The role's own precise
message is not carried by the protocol, not recorded on the attempt, and not
shown by `status` or by `logs` events. It sometimes says "run destroy", and at
times names the host, the address and the fix. The terminal remedy is always
"continue it with bootwright apply". So a deterministic failure becomes a
remedy loop, and the evidence shows the same failure repeated twice. Several
cancellation causes reach the attempt only as context errors, and only
`Canceled` is classified: - a run deadline expiring; - a log fault cancelling
the run; - a hangup; - a reboot. The others become `unknown` with no recorded
reason. The status explanation then says the outcome "was not recorded" even
when `canceled` was. Status cannot tell a live run from an orphaned one. A
second apply plans against a running operation before the lease refuses it. A
log-root fault discards its errno. Early store or log failures can print an
empty receipt.

Strengths to keep:

- An interrupt after registration still writes the operation's result rows,
  Logs/Follow/Next and the receipt, then one `runtime.interrupted` naming the
  continuation, and exits 130 (internal/cli/results.go:71-87). The diagnostics
  the cancellation made each block report are not repeated.
- Cancellation never abandons work in flight: the scheduler stops admitting
  new work and waits for each running block to record its own outcome
  (scheduler.go:163-185). A canceled or unproved attempt becomes `unknown` and
  is resolved from live evidence before anything else starts.
- `lifecycle.adapter-running` is a model refusal. It names the context, the
  block's description, the adapter operation and the Machine, and says to wait
  or which processes to end (jobs_linux_amd64.go:222-240).
- State-root capacity failures name the errno symbol (ENOSPC, EDQUOT, EFBIG)
  and the free-space remedy instead of reading as damage
  (contextfs/files_linux_amd64.go:41-82).
- Changed-input and moved-basis refusals name what changed and both exits,
  continue or destroy (contexts/refusals.go:51-53, decision.go:350-361,
  reproof.go:131-148).

#### Lane X17

**Operator journeys through a failing destroy, end to end**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** A failing destroy is well guarded
against acting wrongly. Every fresh removal re-proves its basis under the
exclusive lock, checks the controller host, and resolves every unproved block
by observation before it registers. The quiescence gate probes every block and
lists every Machine to stop. Authorization refusals name the consuming steps
and a command that passes. An interrupt after registration still writes the
result, the Next command and the receipt, and exits 130. A failed destroy is
replaced by a fresh removal of what it has not proved gone. The unsafe paths
are closed. The operator's view is where it gets thin: - **Failed-block cause
is never stored.** The cause appears once on stderr for the invocation that
hit it. `CompleteAttempt` stores no failure, the event log records only
`outcome failed`, and `status` explains only unknown or running blocks. Once
the terminal scrolls away, a [FAIL] row has no why outside the root-owned raw
output. - **Diagnostics name no block.** Concurrent block failures print
without a block name and are re-sorted by code and message, so they cannot be
matched to the result rows. - **Unproved reads as live.** `lifecycle.live`
"still in use" is used both for a Machine that is running and for one whose
hypervisor did not answer. The remedy, `machine stop`, cannot work on a dead
host, and the real exit is never named: the orphan-acknowledged context
deletion (D38). - **Paused destroy sends mixed signals.** A destroy paused at
the online boundary shows a green "Destroy paused" headline, an error
diagnostic and exit 1. - **The deletion exit hands off its inventory.** The
orphan-acknowledged deletion names `status` and `diff` as its inventory, but
those commands stop working once it completes, and under `--yes` nothing at
all is listed. - **No goldens.** No CLI golden pins a failed, paused, unknown
or refused destroy.

Strengths to keep:

- Every fresh removal resolves every unproved block and proves quiescence
  under the exclusive lock before registering. A refusal there registers
  nothing, and the resolutions are recorded so the next invocation does not
  observe them again.
- proveQuiescent probes every block and reports every Machine to stop with its
  exact machine stop command, rather than one obstacle per repeat.
- The authorization refusals name the consuming steps by plan number and
  description, and the exact passing command. The plan is presented, with
  digests, before the refusal.
- An interrupt after registration still writes result rows, Logs, Follow, Next
  and the receipt, and exits 130 (results.go:71-87). Cancellation waits for
  in-flight blocks instead of abandoning them.
- The physical erase refusals (physicalerase/refusal.go) are the model message
  family: object identity, endpoint, the cause class, what was not done, the
  exact next command, and an alternative exit.

#### Lane X18

**Preflight as failure prevention: which mid-run failures could be refused
before any effect**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** Today `apply` neither runs nor
requires `preflight`. Before registration a fresh apply gets: planning
refusals (missing or changed host-store media, graph and API checks), the
setup receipt and runtime check (`approvedRuntime`), and three admission hooks
wired in cmd/bootwright/wiring_reconciliation.go:400-402. These are the
controller FIPS flag for FIPS clusters, the runtime firewall admission of the
controller's listener sockets, and the libvirt capacity budget (CPU, memory,
disk, including the media writes the apply will make). That capacity admission
is good: it is the same budget code preflight reports, every refusal names a
host and resource, and a refusal leaves no record. Everything else preflight
can see is met only when its block runs: the OpenShift API and ingress name
resolution (in the install block, after the image is built), the Ceph host
prerequisites (hostname, time sync, privilege, DNS, peer names, host
firewall), and provided-host trust. Some classes are never checked before
effect: BMC reachability and credentials (the `machines` stage of preflight
checks nothing), pull-secret and registry reach, controller clock, and foreign
directories in the hosted area. The real runs show this. Six Machines failed
at pre_boot because the management controller returned HTTP 500 (emulated, so
preflight could not have caught it). One run stopped in the machines stage on
a pre-existing hosted-area directory with the wrong mode. Preflight's own
reports are honest, since failed or unknown is never shown as passed. Where
they are thin: SSH failure causes are thrown away ("did not complete"),
pending and unknown share one code, and a fresh context with installed Ceph
hosts can never pass. The pre-boot refusals inside apply are the best part of
the lane: each names its Machine, says that nothing was booted, and gives the
exact continuation.

Strengths to keep:

- Libvirt capacity admission at apply uses the same capacity.Budget code as
  preflight. It also counts the media the apply will write
  (installation.CapacityWrites), names host, pool and resource in each refusal,
  and refuses before registration.
- Media presence, size and digest are proved at planning
  (installation/selection.go:407-425), so missing media never reaches an effect.
- The setup receipt and runtime are proved before registration
  (executor.go:165), and setup is refused with a concrete command.
- Pre-boot refusals (substrate/preboot.go) name the Machine, state that
  nothing was inserted or booted, and give the exact continuation command,
  including --authorize tokens; this is the pattern to generalize.
- Preflight never reports an unobserved or failed probe as passed, and the
  untrusted-host-key row gives the exact machine trust command and the observed
  fingerprint.

#### Lane X19

**Bounds, scale, long runs and repeated cycles**

**How it behaves when things go wrong:** The bounds are mostly checked before
any effect, and the code does this carefully. A fresh apply is admitted only
if the operation area could hold its own first pass, the first pass of the
removal that takes it back, and 1024 extra entries (records.go:60). Every
attempt, retry or resolution is counted before it writes (AdmitAttempt,
store.go:302), so an apply can never eat into its removal's first pass.
Adapter output and JSONL logs live outside the store, with per-file caps. The
attempt log keeps a 32 KiB tail for non-group events, so the outcome line
survives a chatty role. Concurrent failures produce at most about the
scheduler bound of diagnostics, in frozen plan order. The weak side is long
life and the exits: - No command prunes operations (B258). The real limit is
the 8192-entry area bound, not the 1024-operation bound the table advertises.
A 60-block context reaches it after about 18 clean destroy and apply cycles.
The refusal still says "retained the maximum number of lifecycle operations"
and quotes raw byte counts. - The removal's reserve is exactly its first pass
plus one entry. A forced destroy that follows an apply refused at its reserve
therefore cannot retry even one failed block. Its remedy is `context delete
--purge --allow-orphans`. - An adapter run that passes its own 2 h or 6 h
deadline is recorded `unknown`, and the scheduler drops its cause, so nothing
tells the operator a deadline expired. - Byte admission is a flat 16 MiB
whatever the plan's size, so a large plan admitted near the byte line can
refuse its first attempt. - Log retention runs only when an operation
registers, and the output room is measured once per invocation. The bounds are
enforced ad hoc in several functions, each with its own wording. Only the
1024-operation bound has a remedy chosen per context (retainedExit).

Strengths to keep:

- Admission is done before any effect, from what the plan needs
  (AdmissionEntries, AdmissionBytes, admitOperations), and AdmitAttempt counts
  every in-flight attempt, so an apply never starves its removal's first pass.
- The remedy at the retained-operation bound is chosen per context:
  retainedExit reads the evidence and idle claims and names destroy, delete, or
  delete with --allow-orphans plus a warning about reusing the name.
- Logs and adapter output live outside the store and have per-file caps (128
  KiB attempt log, 4 MiB output). However verbose a role is, it never consumes
  record space.
- The attempt log keeps a 32 KiB tail free of group records, so the outcome
  event survives a chatty run, and Close writes an explicit truncation marker.
- The scheduler stops new starts after the first failure in an invocation and
  orders causes by frozen plan position, which bounds diagnostic volume at about
  the concurrency bound, even for 256-block plans.
